readings.title: Practice 1: Talking with our hands
readings.qtype: Yes/No/Not Given (1–4) + Summary, word list (5–9) + Multiple choice A–D (10–14)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 3 darajasi)
text: Watch anyone speaking on the telephone and you will probably see their hands moving, even though the listener cannot see them. For a long time, this was treated as a curious habit, a kind of nervous decoration added to the real business of speech. In my view, that explanation has always been unconvincing. If gestures existed only to help listeners, we would expect people to stop gesturing as soon as nobody could see them. They do not. Nor is the habit limited to a few especially expressive individuals; almost everyone does it, whatever their personality or background.

The strongest evidence comes from people who have never seen a gesture at all. In one well-known study, researchers asked children who had been blind from birth to describe routes and to explain simple puzzles. The children moved their hands as they spoke, using much the same kinds of movements as sighted children, and they did so even when they knew that their listener was also blind. Gesture, it seems, is not simply copied from others. The researchers also noted that the children gestured more when the task was harder, which is exactly what one would expect if gesture were helping them to think. It appears to be part of the way that speakers organise what they want to say.

This idea is supported by experiments in which people are prevented from moving their hands. When speakers are asked to sit on their hands or hold an object while describing a picture, they tend to pause more often and to have greater difficulty finding words, especially words for shapes, directions and movements. Not every study has found this effect, and its size varies considerably from one experiment to another. Nevertheless, the general pattern suggests that gesture helps speakers to find language, not just to deliver it.

Children offer a further window on the relationship. Long before they can produce two-word sentences, many toddlers combine a single word with a pointing gesture: they say 'cup' while pointing at their mother, meaning something like 'Mummy's cup'. Researchers who have followed children over several months report that those who produce these word-plus-gesture combinations early also tend to begin speaking in two-word sentences earlier. Gesture, in other words, may allow children to express an idea before they have the grammar to put it into words. Parents, of course, respond to these combinations, often by turning the idea into a full sentence — 'Yes, that's Mummy's cup' — so gesture may also invite exactly the kind of language that children need to hear.

None of this means that gestures are the same everywhere. Travellers quickly discover that a hand signal which is harmless at home can be rude elsewhere, and even the way people point differs between cultures: in some communities, people point with their lips or chin rather than with a finger. The amount of gesturing also varies. Speakers of some languages are famous for using their hands a great deal, although the popular belief that certain nationalities gesture more than others has been examined far less carefully than one might expect.

What are the practical lessons? Teachers have begun to take gesture seriously. In classroom studies, children who were taught a maths strategy with both words and gestures remembered it better several weeks later than children who were taught with words alone. I would not go so far as to say that every lesson should be accompanied by carefully planned hand movements; forced gestures can distract as much as they help. But teachers who fold their arms while explaining a difficult idea may be making it harder for their students than necessary.

Language learners, too, might benefit. A learner who cannot remember a word can often keep a conversation going by describing it with their hands, and the listener's response frequently supplies the missing word. Rather than being a sign of weakness, this is exactly the kind of strategy that successful communicators use. The hands, it turns out, are not an accessory to speech. They are one of the places where speech begins.
glossary: toddler — endi yura boshlagan bola (1–3 yosh)
accessory — qo'shimcha bezak, ikkinchi darajali narsa
paraphrases: mainly for the benefit of the listener
not always done with the hand

readings.title: Practice 2: Is texting ruining young people's writing?
readings.qtype: Yes/No/Not Given (1–4) + Summary, word list (5–9) + Multiple choice A–D (10–14)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 3 darajasi)
text: Every few years, a newspaper announces that young people can no longer write. The cause changes — television, then computer games, now mobile phones — but the complaint remains the same. Text messages, with their missing vowels, abbreviations and absent punctuation, are currently blamed for everything from poor spelling in school essays to the decline of the handwritten letter. It is an easy argument to make, and in my view it is largely mistaken.

To begin with, the features that alarm critics are not new. Abbreviations such as 'etc.' and 'Mr' have been used for centuries, and Victorian telegrams, which were charged by the word, were at least as compressed as any modern text message. Word puzzles that replace words with letters and numbers were popular long before the first mobile phone. What is new is the quantity: young people today probably write more words each day than any previous generation of teenagers, even if many of those words are short.

Researchers have tested the claim directly. In several studies with primary-school children, those who used more textisms — the abbreviations typical of text messages — did not have worse spelling than their classmates. In some cases, the opposite was true: children who were good at producing textisms were also better at reading and spelling. This makes sense when one considers that writing 'gr8' for 'great' requires a child to understand how sounds relate to letters. You cannot break a rule creatively unless you know what the rule is.

That said, the picture is not entirely positive. Studies of older teenagers and university students have produced more mixed results, and some teachers report that informal features occasionally appear in formal work. Such slips are real, but they tend to be fairly rare, and they are usually corrected once they are pointed out. The more important skill, it seems to me, is not avoiding informal writing altogether but knowing when it is appropriate.

Linguists call this skill register awareness: the ability to adjust one's language to suit the situation. Every competent speaker does this constantly. We do not speak to a job interviewer in the same way that we speak to a younger brother, and nobody concludes from our relaxed conversations at home that we are unable to speak politely. Written language is no different. A student who writes 'c u l8r' to a friend and a carefully structured paragraph in an exam is not confused; they are switching between registers, just as adults do. The same person may use three or four different registers in a single afternoon — in a lecture, in a message to a friend, on the phone to a bank — without noticing that they have done anything unusual.

Where, then, should concern be directed? If there is a genuine problem, it may lie less in how young people write than in how much they read. Short messages, however frequent, do not expose readers to the long, complex sentences found in books and quality journalism. A teenager who writes hundreds of messages a day but never reads anything longer than a paragraph may well struggle when asked to produce an extended argument. The solution, however, is not to ban phones but to make sure that sustained reading remains part of every young person's week. Reading and writing develop together, and the vocabulary and sentence patterns that students meet in books are the ones they later reproduce in their own essays.

Language has always changed, and older generations have always worried about it. Texting has added a new variety of English to the many that already exist; it has not replaced the others. Rather than treating it as a threat, schools could use it as a starting point for discussing how and why we choose different words for different audiences. A pupil who can explain why 'u' is acceptable in a message but not in a job application has understood something important about language.

readings.title: Practice 3 (uyga): Learning a language as an adult — is it too late?
readings.qtype: Multiple choice A–D (1–4) + Summary, word list (5–9) + Yes/No/Not Given (10–14)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 3 darajasi), uy vazifasi
text: It is widely believed that children are better language learners than adults. The belief is so common that many adults never start learning a language at all, assuming that the chance has passed. There is some truth in the idea, but it has been exaggerated, and the way it is usually expressed hides several important distinctions.

The first distinction is between the speed of learning and the final level reached. When researchers compare children and adults over the first months of learning, adults usually make faster progress. They can apply rules consciously, use a dictionary, and draw on what they already know about how languages work. In classroom studies lasting a year or two, teenagers and adults often do better than young children on tests of grammar and reading. Older learners also tend to be better at learning vocabulary quickly. Children's advantage appears only in the long term: those who start young and spend many years surrounded by a language are much more likely to end up sounding like native speakers.

The second distinction concerns which part of language we are talking about. Pronunciation is where age seems to matter most. People who begin learning a language after their early teens very rarely lose their foreign accent completely, however long they live in the new country. Even so, many people with a noticeable accent speak fluently and are perfectly easy to understand, and for most purposes that is what matters. Grammar shows a weaker connection with age, and vocabulary shows little connection at all: adults continue to learn new words in their first language throughout their lives, and there is no obvious reason why a second language should be different.

A third distinction is between learning a language and living in it. Much of the research that supports the idea of a 'critical period' comes from immigrants, whose age on arrival is compared with their eventual level. But age on arrival is linked to many other factors. A child who arrives at eight goes to a local school, makes local friends and hears the language all day. An adult who arrives at thirty may work long hours with people who speak their first language, and may feel embarrassed about making mistakes. It is difficult to know how much of the adult's lower final level is caused by the brain and how much by circumstances.

One large online study, which collected grammar test results from hundreds of thousands of people, suggested that the ability to learn grammar remains strong until late adolescence and declines only after that. The researchers were careful to point out that this does not mean adults cannot learn grammar well; it means that reaching a native-like level becomes gradually less likely, not impossible. In my opinion, this is the most useful way to think about age: as something that changes the odds rather than something that closes a door.

What does this mean for an adult who wants to learn a language? First, the goal matters. If the aim is to sound exactly like a native speaker, starting late is a genuine disadvantage. If the aim is to communicate effectively, read, work or study in the language, adults are in a strong position, especially at the beginning. Second, adults should make use of their strengths: their ability to organise their study, to understand explanations and to notice patterns. Third, they should try to recreate some of the conditions children enjoy — plenty of exposure, meaningful conversation and, perhaps most importantly, a willingness to make mistakes without feeling foolish.

It is sometimes said that adults learn languages badly because they are afraid of looking silly. There may be something in this. Children rarely worry about whether their sentences are correct; they simply want to be understood. Adults, by contrast, often stay silent rather than risk an error, and silence is the one thing that guarantees no progress. Adults who can recover a little of that attitude may find that the door they thought had closed was never really locked.

intro: Section 3 — o'quv mavzusidagi suhbat: odatda talaba(lar) va o'qituvchi (tutor), ba'zan uch kishi. Unda faqat ma'lumot emas, FIKR va BAHO ham bo'ladi: "a bit dull", "went down well", "I wasn't sure they could be justified". 6.0 darajasida Section 3 ko'pincha uch savol turidan iborat: TWO letters, matching va short answer.

Tayyorlanish vaqtini uchga bo'ling. TWO letters: savol o'zagidagi kalit g'oyani tagiga chizing ("WILL students do", "MUST check", "IMPRESSIVE according to the tutor"). Matching: sarlavha va variantlardagi kalit so'zlarni belgilang (repetitive, long time to write, shorter, well structured, relevant, popular). Short answer: so'z chegarasini doiraga oling.

Choose TWO letters (A–E): beshta variantning deyarli hammasi suhbatda tilga olinadi. Uch variant tuzoq bo'ladi: taklif qilinib RAD ETILADI ("something from one of the textbooks" → "a much better idea"), kelajakdagi yoki boshqa ishga tegishli bo'ladi ("the starting point for a whole other piece of work"), yoki salbiy baholanadi. Javoblar variantlar tartibida emas, suhbat tartibida keladi. Har harf — alohida ball; ikkala harfni istalgan tartibda yozish mumkin.

Matching (A–F): savollar (5, 6, 7, 8) suhbat tartibida keladi, variantlar esa aralash. 6 variantdan 4 tasi kerak — 2 tasi ortiqcha. Har bir savol bo'yicha gapiruvchi odatda bir nechta narsa aytadi: masalan, "History of English" haqida "a bit dull" ham, "clearly sequenced" ham aytiladi — faqat ikkinchisi ro'yxatda bor.

Suhbatdagi fikr o'zgarishi: talaba bir narsani aytadi, tutor to'g'rilaydi ("No — that's an obvious one"). Oxirgi, kelishilgan fikr javob bo'ladi. "But", "though", "whereas", "actually" so'zlaridan keyin diqqatni kuchaytiring.

Short answer: savolga to'g'ridan-to'g'ri javob; NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS — "digital recorders" (2 so'z) to'g'ri, "department's digital recorders" — 3 so'z, xato. Ko'plik kalitda ko'pincha qavs bilan beriladi: mobile phone(s).
presentation: TWO letters da ikkala harfni bitta katakka yozamanmi?
Yo'q. Imtihonda 1 va 2 alohida katak: har biriga bitta harf, tartib ahamiyatsiz (A, D yoki D, A).
Uchala variant ham eshitildi, qaysini tanlayman?
Qaysi biri qabul qilinganini tinglang. "That's a much better idea", "that's also important" — tasdiq; "No", "I wouldn't worry about" — rad.
Matching da bitta harfni ikki marta yozsam bo'ladimi?
Bu turdagi ro'yxatda odatda har harf bir marta. Ko'rsatmani o'qing: "Choose FOUR answers from the box".
Matching savollari tartibdami?
Ha — 5, 6, 7, 8 suhbat tartibida. Variantlar (A–F) tartibda emas.
Kim gapirayotganini qanday bilaman?
Ismlar boshida aytiladi (Amanda, Dr White). Savolda "according to the tutor" bo'lsa, faqat tutor fikri hisobga olinadi.
Short answer da artikl yozamanmi?
Shart emas. "mobile phones" yetarli — "the mobile phones" chegarani buzishi mumkin.

listenings.title: Student's Book, Track 10: Amanda's assignment (Q1–4)
listenings.qtype: Multiple choice — Choose TWO letters (A–E), Section 3, 1-qism
intro: Amanda o'z tutori Dr White bilan talaffuz bo'yicha topshirig'ini muhokama qiladi. SB 2-mashq: tinglashdan oldin savol o'zagidagi kalit g'oyani tagiga chizing (variantlarni emas): "WILL students do", "MUST check".
Beshta variantning ko'pi eshitiladi — qaysi biri qabul qilinib, qaysi biri rad etilganini belgilab boring. Savollar sahifasi quyida rasm sifatida.

tasks.title: Questions 1–4
tasks.type: Choose TWO letters, A–E
tasks.instr: Har savol uchun ikkita harf. Javoblar variantlar tartibida emas, suhbat tartibida keladi.
items: 1–2 Which TWO activities will students do as part of Amanda's assignment? A) analyse their own speech B) record other students' speech C) read something from a book D) repeat part of a lecture E) remember part of a lecture

3–4 Which TWO features must Amanda check when she chooses the extract? A) the time it takes to read B) the overall organisation C) the number of words D) the number of sentences E) the inclusion of key ideas
why: A: "record themselves ... then listen back and see where their weaknesses lie". D: "look up one of my lectures on the website and find a suitable extract" — talabalar uni ovoz chiqarib o'qiydi. Tuzoqlar: B — "peer evaluation" (sheriklarni baholash, ularni yozib olish emas); C — "one of the textbooks" taklifi "a much better idea" bilan almashtirilgan; E — "it isn't a memory test".

B: "a clear, well-structured passage". E: "what you do need are some obvious main points". Tuzoqlar: A — "taking a while to make the selection" (Amandaning vaqti, o'qish vaqti emas); C — "shouldn't consist entirely of short words" (so'zlar soni emas, turi); D — "I wouldn't worry about how many sentences there are".
tasks.note: Ikkala savolda ham beshta variantning to'rttasi yoki beshtasi tilga olinadi. O'quvchilar har variant yoniga ✓ (qabul) yoki ✗ (rad) qo'yib tinglasin — kalitdagi izohlar ham shu gaplarni ko'rsatadi.

listenings.title: Student's Book, Track 11: Choosing a lecture (Q5–10)
intro: Dr White Amandaga qaysi ma'ruzadan parcha olishni tavsiya qiladi. SB 4-mashq: 6 variant, 4 savol — 2 tasi ortiqcha. Variantlardagi kalit so'zlarni tagiga chizing.
SB 5-mashq: 9–10 savollar — NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS. Savol: "Which TWO pieces of equipment will the students use?"

tasks.title: Questions 5–8 — Lectures
tasks.type: Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F
tasks.instr: Ma'ruzalar suhbatda tartib bilan keladi; har biri haqida ikki-uch fikr aytiladi — ro'yxatdagisini tanlang.
box: B It took a long time to write.
C It was shorter than the others.
items: 5 History of English
6 Gestures and signs
7 Intonation patterns
8 Language and rhythm
why: "A lot of information which was clearly sequenced and presented". Tuzoq: "The topic's a bit dull" — ro'yxatda yo'q.
"The lecture on gestures and signs certainly went down well" + Amanda: "I really liked that one". Tuzoq: E — "not sure that the content is related".

"The topic's certainly more closely linked to the whole area of pronunciation". Tuzoqlar: B — "I didn't take long to put that together" (teskari); A — "watch out in case there are too many examples" (ogohlantirish, fakt emas).
"One of my mini-lectures" + "I wouldn't have to spend too much time going through the content"; tutor: "whereas the one on intonation patterns was a lot longer".
tasks.note: 7-savol — asosiy tuzoq: tutor "didn't take long" deydi. B ni tanlagan o'quvchiga "didn't" ni ko'rsating.

tasks.title: Questions 9–10
tasks.type: Answer the question. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: Which TWO pieces of equipment will the students use in the study?
why: "They could use mobile phones, couldn't they? Though the sound quality may not be good on all of them" — sifat haqida shubha bor, lekin ishlatiladi.
"We can also bring in some of the department's digital recorders". "Department's digital recorders" — 3 so'z, chegara buziladi.
tasks.note: Javoblar istalgan tartibda qabul qilinadi (9 — digital recorders, 10 — mobile phones ham to'g'ri).

listenings.title: Student's Book: recording script (Track 10–11) — ustoz uchun
intro: Tekshiruvdan keyin ekranga chiqaring. 1–4 savollar uchun har variant qayerda tilga olinganini va qabul/rad etilganini belgilang.

listenings.title: Workbook, Track 4: Beth's dissertation (Q1–10)
listenings.qtype: TWO letters + Matching + Short answer — imtihon rejimi
intro: Talaba Beth tutori bilan "Communication Skills in the Workplace" dissertatsiyasi haqida gaplashadi. Avval Workbook 1-mashqi: suhbat qanday dissertatsiya haqida?
Keyin imtihondagidek: tayyorlanish vaqti, audio BIR MARTA, 10 savol.

tasks.title: 1-mashq: suhbat nima haqida?
tasks.type: Choose A, B or C
tasks.instr: Barcha savollarga ko'z yugurting: "did Beth include", "were impressive", "comments about each section", "in her conclusion".
items: 1 What are the speakers talking about? A) a dissertation the student is planning B) a dissertation the student is writing C) a dissertation the student has completed
why: Savollar o'tgan zamonda ("did Beth include", "were impressive") va xulosa haqida — ish tugagan. Audioda tutor oxirida: "this is a good piece of work. Well done."

tasks.title: Questions 1–4
tasks.type: Choose TWO letters, A–E
tasks.instr: 3–4 savolda faqat TUTOR fikri: "impressive, according to the tutor".
items: 1–2 Which TWO areas of work did Beth include in her dissertation? A) retail B) banking C) call centres D) tourism E) translation

3–4 Which TWO aspects of the dissertation were impressive, according to the tutor? A) summary of academic research B) analysis of videos C) observation of live interactions D) interviews E) analysis of data on the outcomes
why: A: "the retail sector had to be in there". D: "that led you to the idea of tourist guides". Tuzoqlar: B — "banking would probably lead to the same sort of results as retail" (kiritilmagan); C — "I decided to spread the focus away"; E — "the starting point for a whole other piece of work".

C: "your analysis from watching people in action was very effective". D: intervyular — "it's very interesting to compare what people think they're doing with the way they're actually communicating. I was very struck by that aspect". Tuzoqlar: A — "a bit more on the academic research ... would have been good"; B — "it would have been good if you could have filmed people" (qilinmagan); E — "it would be fascinating to get data on the outcomes" (kelajak uchun g'oya).
tasks.note: 3–4 savol — "would have been good" tuzog'i: bu qilinMAGAN ish haqida. Doskada "would have + V3" = amalga oshmagan narsa ekanini ko'rsating.

tasks.title: Questions 5–8 — Sections of Dissertation
tasks.type: Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F
tasks.instr: Har bo'lim haqida tutor ham, Beth ham gapiradi. Kelishilgan baho — javob.
box: A There is not enough evidence.
C It highlights a real problem.
D It is particularly well organised.
E There are too many examples.
items: 5 Dealing with Complaints
6 Collaborating with Colleagues
7 Interacting with Managers
8 Giving Instructions
why: "This section had some really original thinking on your part"; Beth: "come up with something fresh".
"I didn't feel that your conclusions were really backed up by the research you did" + "I wasn't sure they could be justified by the examples". Tuzoq: E — misollar ko'p emas, ular dalil bo'la olmagan.
"Your conclusions there point to something that causes all sorts of trouble in organisations".
"The Giving Instructions section was very well put together". Tuzoq: E — "lots of examples" maqtov sifatida; B — "a conclusion that made logical sense" (teskari).

tasks.title: Questions 9–10
tasks.type: Answer the question. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: Which TWO aspects of communication does Beth emphasise in her conclusion?
why: "You see Listening Skills as a much bigger issue". Tuzoq: "Writing Skills" — asosiy qismda, xulosada emas.
"There are lots of instances where this is less of an issue than Formal Language". Tuzoq: "Grammatical Accuracy" — tutor taklif qiladi, Beth "up to a point" deb cheklaydi.
tasks.note: Javoblar istalgan tartibda. 10-savolda ko'p o'quvchi "grammatical accuracy" yozadi — "Well, up to a point, but..." ni skriptda ko'rsating.

listenings.title: Workbook: recording script (Track 4) — ustoz uchun
intro: Skript bilan qayta tinglashda xato qilingan savollarning gapini topishga ishlatiladi. "would have been good" va "up to a point" gaplarini alohida belgilang.

listenings.title: Jony Academy mashqi: Planning a group presentation (Q1–10)
intro: Ikki talaba (Kamola va Daniel) "Communication Skills" kursi uchun guruh taqdimotini tutor bilan muhokama qiladi. Ustoz TUTOR rolini o'qiydi, ikki kuchli o'quvchi — KAMOLA va DANIEL. Qolganlar BIR MARTA tinglaydi.
Tayyorlanish: 1 daqiqa. Ko'rsatmalar: Q1–4 — Choose TWO letters; Q5–8 — Choose FOUR answers from the box (A–F); Q9–10 — NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS.
transcript: TUTOR: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your group presentation for the Communication Skills module?
KAMOLA: Yes. We've chosen our topic — communication in online meetings.
TUTOR: Good choice. Everyone has had some experience of those now. How are you planning to collect your data?
DANIEL: Well, our first idea was to record some real meetings at the companies where we do our part-time jobs, and then analyse them.
TUTOR: Hmm. You'd need everyone's permission for that, and companies are often worried about privacy.
KAMOLA: That's exactly what my manager said, so we've dropped that idea. Instead, we're going to put a short questionnaire online and send the link to students and staff.
TUTOR: Fine. And will that be enough on its own?
DANIEL: We thought about interviewing some managers as well, but most of them told us they simply don't have time this month.
KAMOLA: So we're going to run a focus group instead — six or seven students who use online meetings every week, discussing their experiences for about an hour.
TUTOR: That should give you some rich detail. Last year's group observed online lessons, but I think your approach suits your topic better.
TUTOR: Now, I've read the plan you sent me. Can I be honest about it?
DANIEL: Of course.

TUTOR: The length is fine — fifteen minutes is exactly what's required, so don't worry about that. And I know the deadline is close, but you've got plenty of time. My main concern is that you're trying to cover too much. You've listed eight different topics. In fifteen minutes you'd only have time to mention each one.
KAMOLA: So we should choose three or four?

TUTOR: Four at most. The other thing is your reading list. A lot of the articles on it were written before most people had ever used video calls. The situation has changed completely since then, so look for more recent research.
DANIEL: OK. What about the number of people answering our questionnaire? We're hoping for about forty.
TUTOR: Forty is perfectly reasonable for a student project.
TUTOR: So, which four sections have you decided on?

KAMOLA: First, camera use — whether people keep their cameras on or off. Most of our friends assumed that everyone keeps the camera on. But in our small trial, more than half the people switched it off. I think that's going to shock people.
TUTOR: Yes, that could well be the most unexpected part for your audience. Good.
DANIEL: Then interrupting. In online meetings, people either talk over each other or nobody speaks at all.
TUTOR: That's hard to explain with slides alone.
DANIEL: We know. So Kamola and I are going to act out a short meeting — two minutes, one version where everyone interrupts and one with clear turn-taking.
KAMOLA: We thought about putting it at the very end, but it's better in the middle, to wake everyone up.
TUTOR: The audience will enjoy that.
KAMOLA: Third, the chat box — how people use written messages during a meeting.
TUTOR: Hmm. Isn't a lot of that already covered in your section on interrupting? People type in the chat when they can't get a word in.
KAMOLA: Yes, I suppose there is some repetition there.
TUTOR: Think about how to separate the two. I wouldn't worry about finding more figures for it, though — you've got plenty.
DANIEL: And finally, background noise — dogs barking, traffic, that kind of thing.
TUTOR: It's a real issue, but it's more technical than the others.
DANIEL: Yes, we've agreed that if we're running over fifteen minutes in rehearsal, that's the section we'll drop.
TUTOR: Sensible. Right — before Friday, could you send me a couple of things?
KAMOLA: The slides?
TUTOR: No, not yet — I'll look at those next week. First, I'd like to see your new reading list, with the recent articles.
DANIEL: OK, the reading list.
TUTOR: And the questionnaire itself, before you put it online. I'd like to check the wording of the questions.
KAMOLA: Of course. We'll send both on Thursday.
TUTOR: Excellent. Good luck with it.

tasks.title: Questions 1–4
tasks.type: Choose TWO letters, A–E
tasks.instr: Rad etilgan variantlarni ✗ bilan belgilab boring.
items: 1–2 Which TWO methods will the students use to collect data? A) an online questionnaire B) recordings of real meetings C) interviews with managers D) observation of online lessons E) a focus group

3–4 Which TWO problems does the tutor mention about the students' plan? A) It covers too many topics. B) The number of people in the survey is too small. C) There is not enough time before the deadline. D) The presentation will be too long. E) Some of the sources are out of date.
why: A: "we're going to put a short questionnaire online". E: "we're going to run a focus group instead". Tuzoqlar: B — "we've dropped that idea"; C — menejerlarning vaqti yo'q; D — o'tgan yilgi guruh qilgan.

A: "you're trying to cover too much. You've listed eight different topics". E: "a lot of the articles ... were written before most people had ever used video calls". Tuzoqlar: B — "forty is perfectly reasonable"; C — "you've got plenty of time"; D — "the length is fine".

tasks.title: Questions 5–8 — Sections of the presentation
tasks.type: Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F
tasks.instr: Bo'limlar suhbatda tartib bilan keladi.
box: B It will probably surprise the audience.
C It should be moved to the end.
D It overlaps with another section.
E It will include a short demonstration.
F It may be left out.
items: 5 Camera use
6 Interrupting
7 Chat box
8 Background noise
why: "I think that's going to shock people" + tutor: "the most unexpected part for your audience".
"We're going to act out a short meeting — two minutes". Tuzoq: C — "we thought about putting it at the very end, but it's better in the middle".
"Isn't a lot of that already covered in your section on interrupting?" — "there is some repetition". Tuzoq: A — "I wouldn't worry about finding more figures".
"If we're running over fifteen minutes in rehearsal, that's the section we'll drop".

tasks.title: Questions 9–10
tasks.type: Answer the question. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: Which TWO things will the students send to the tutor before Friday?
why: "First, I'd like to see your new reading list". "New reading list" — 3 so'z; "reading list" yozing.
"And the questionnaire itself, before you put it online". Tuzoq: "The slides?" — "No, not yet".
tasks.note: Javoblar istalgan tartibda. 9-savolda "new reading list" (3 so'z) — chegara buziladi, shuning uchun 0 ball.

homework_intro: Bugun Section 3 da uch savol turini ketma-ket yechdik: TWO letters, matching va short answer. Eng ko'p ball rad etilgan variantlarda va paraphrase'da yo'qoladi.
Birinchi vazifa — shadowing: SB Track 10 ni qo'yib, Amandaning gaplarini ovoz bilan birga takrorlang (kamida 3 marta). Keyin Amanda rolini audiosiz o'qib, ovozli xabar qilib guruhga yuboring.

Ikkinchi vazifa — diktant: WB Track 4 ning ikkinchi qismini ("Now, looking at the content of your dissertation..." dan "Pause" gacha) to'xtatib-to'xtatib yozing, keyin skript rasmi bilan tekshiring va xatolarni qizil bilan belgilang.

Uchinchi vazifa — paraphrase ro'yxati: SB Track 11 va WB Track 4 ni skriptsiz qayta tinglab, 5–8 savollardagi har bir variant (A–F) audioda qanday aytilganini yozing (masalan, popular → went down well). Xatolar daftariga ham qo'shing.

homework.title: Shadowing: SB Track 10 (Amanda)
homework.instr: 3 marta audio bilan birga, keyin audiosiz; ovozli xabar guruhga.
homework.answers: Ustoz ohang, urg'u va to'xtashlarni tekshiradi.

homework.title: Diktant: WB Track 4 (2-qism)
homework.instr: Bo'limlar haqidagi qismni to'xtatib yozish, skript bilan tekshirish.
homework.answers: Skript rasmi bo'yicha o'zi tekshiradi; ustoz 3 ta gapni so'raydi.

homework.title: Paraphrase ro'yxati: matching variantlari
homework.instr: SB Track 11 va WB Track 4: har variant uchun audiodagi ibora.
homework.answers: Kamida 8 juftlik; keyingi darsda og'zaki tekshiriladi.

lessons.title: Unit 4 Reading — Passage 1: True / False / Not Given + Note completion + Short answer
lessons.grammar_topic: Uch savol turi bitta passage'da: TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN + Note completion + Short-answer questions
lessons.vocab_topic: Unit 4 (New media) — internet, ilm-fan va onlayn jamiyat
lessons.book_ref: Complete IELTS Bands 5–6.5: Student's Book, Unit 4, 37–40-betlar (Reading Section 1); Workbook, Unit 4, 24–26-betlar. Practice 1–3 — Jony Academy matnlari.
objectives: Bitta passage'da uch savol guruhi kelganda (1–6, 7–10, 11–13) har guruh matnning qaysi qismiga tegishli ekanini 2 daqiqada belgilash ("xarita" usuli).
TRUE, FALSE va NOT GIVEN ni isbot gap bilan ajratish; "so'z bor, da'vo yo'q" tuzog'ini tanish.
Note completion'da notes sarlavhasidan kerakli xatboshini topish va bo'shliq turini (ot, fe'l, sifat, ko'plik) oldindan aytish.
Short-answer savollarida savol so'ziga qarab javob turini aniqlash: Whose → shaxs/nom, Which publication → nom, What type → ot birikmasi.
Javobni matndan aynan ko'chirish va so'z chegarasiga (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS / AND/OR A NUMBER) rioya qilish.
materials: Student's Book, Unit 4, 37–40-betlar (Reading Section 1: "The World Wide Web from its origins") — sinfda birga ishlanadi.
Workbook, Unit 4, 24–26-betlar ("Is constant use of electronic media changing our minds?") — mustaqil mashq.
Practice 1–3 matnlari chop etilgan varaqlar (har o'quvchiga) — pastdagi Reading bo'limidan.
Taymer: Passage 1 uchun 17–20 daqiqa normasi doskaga yoziladi.
Doskada uch ustun: "T/F/NG → qaysi xatboshilar?", "Notes → sarlavha qaysi qismga?", "Short answer → savol so'zi → javob turi".
timeline: Kirish
Savol: "Yangiliklarni, ma'lumotni va dam olishni qaysi media orqali olasiz?" — SB 37-bet ro'yxati bo'yicha 3–4 o'quvchi javob beradi.
Uch savol turi birga
Ustoz doskada: xarita usuli; T/F/NG, note completion va short answer qoidalari; vaqt taqsimoti; tipik xatolar.

17 daqiqa mustaqil, keyin javoblar izoh bilan tekshiriladi.
Practice 1

intro: Oldingi darslarda passage'da ikki savol turi bor edi. Bugun — uchta: TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN (1–6), note completion (7–10) va short-answer questions (11–13). IELTS'da bu juda keng tarqalgan kombinatsiya.

Birinchi qadam — XARITA. Matnni o'qishdan oldin uchala guruhga 2 daqiqa ko'z yugurtiring. Student's Book'da 1–6 matnning birinchi yarmi (Berners-Lee, CERN, galaktikalar loyihasi), 7–10 — notes sarlavhasi "Social networks and internet use", ya'ni ijtimoiy tarmoqlar tadqiqoti xatboshisi, 11–13 — oxirgi xatboshi (jurnalistlar, bloggerlar, Nature).

T/F/NG: savoldagi kalit so'zni (ism, raqam, noyob so'z) belgilang va matndan toping. Savollar matn tartibida keladi. Eslatma: "so'z bor — da'vo yo'q" bo'lsa, NOT GIVEN (masalan, matnda "political campaigning" bor, lekin Berners-Lee siyosat bilan shug'ullangani haqida gap yo'q).

Note completion: notes sarlavhasi kerakli xatboshini ko'rsatadi. Har bo'shliqqa qanday so'z kerakligini oldindan ayting: "the ___ of social networks" — ot; "Most ___ intended for" — ko'plikdagi ot. Notes'dagi so'zlar matnda paraphrase bilan keladi ("limited number of people" = "a few specific friends").

Short-answer questions: savol so'zi javob turini aytadi. "Whose writing...?" — kishilar guruhi; "What type of writing...?" — ot birikmasi; "Which publication...?" — nom. Javob matndan aynan olinadi va savoldagi so'zlarni takrorlamaydi.

So'z chegarasi uchala guruhda ham muhim: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS — ikki so'zdan oshsa, javob to'g'ri bo'lsa ham 0 ball. Workbook'da chegara boshqacha: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER ("100,000 children" — raqam + bitta so'z).
Vaqt: 17–20 daqiqa. Taxminiy taqsimot: T/F/NG — 7 daqiqa, notes — 5 daqiqa, short answer — 4 daqiqa, tekshiruv — 2 daqiqa. Qiyin savolda 2 daqiqadan ko'p turmang.
formulas: T/F/NG kalit so'zlarini belgilang va tartib bilan ishlang
Short answer: savol so'zi → javob turi
Javobni matndan aynan ko'chiring va sanang
presentation: Qaysi guruhdan boshlayman?
Odatda tartib bilan. Lekin short answer'lar ko'pincha matn oxirida — xaritada buni oldindan belgilang.
Notes va short answer'lar ham matn tartibidami?
Guruh ichida odatda (USUALLY) ha. Lekin guruhlar orasida sakrash bo'lishi mumkin: Workbook'da 11–13 matnning oxirgi qismidan, 7–10 esa o'rtasidan.
Short answer'da gap bilan javob yozsam bo'ladimi?
Yo'q. Faqat kerakli 1–2 so'z: "Whose writing improves?" → "bloggers", "The bloggers' writing" emas.
Notes'da so'z matnda boshqacha shaklda bo'lsa-chi?
Javob matndan aynan ko'chiriladi. Grammatika mos kelmasa — ehtimol boshqa so'zni topgansiz.
FALSE va NOT GIVEN ni qanday ajrataman?
FALSE — matnda qarshi isbot gap bor. NOT GIVEN — isbot gap umuman yo'q; mavzu bo'lishi mumkin, da'vo yo'q.
Raqam so'z hisoblanadimi?
"AND/OR A NUMBER" bo'lsa, raqam alohida hisoblanadi: "100,000 children" — to'g'ri. Faqat "TWO WORDS" bo'lsa, raqam ham so'z hisoblanadi.
notes: Bu darsda asosiy yangilik — uchinchi savol turi (short answer). 5.0 da uni alohida o'rgangan edik; endi uni T/F/NG va notes bilan bitta passage'da, bitta vaqt ichida yechamiz.
Har javobdan keyin ikki savol bering: "isbot qaysi gapda?" va "savol yoki notes'dagi qaysi so'z matnda qanday aytilgan?"
Kuchli o'quvchilarga: xaritani 2 daqiqada chizib, har guruh qaysi xatboshilarga to'g'ri kelishini oldindan aytish; Workbook'ni 15 daqiqada ishlash.

Savol "Whose" — kimlar; ortiqcha so'z chegarani buzadi
Savoldagi fe'lni takrorlash shart emas, uch so'z — 0 ball
Short answer'ni butun gap bilan yozish

how: CORE — internet va media mavzusidagi asosiy so'zlar; STRONG — ilmiy va tahliliy matnlar so'zlari; SUPER — akademik iboralar.

readings.title: Practice 1: Podcasts — radio for the internet age
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 1 darajasi)
text: In 2004, a journalist writing for a British newspaper was looking for a name for a new kind of radio. Programmes could now be recorded as digital files and downloaded from the internet onto portable music players, so listeners no longer had to tune in at a fixed time. Among the names he suggested was 'podcasting', a combination of 'iPod', the most popular music player of the day, and 'broadcasting'. The word caught on so quickly that, within a year, it had been chosen as word of the year by a major American dictionary.

At first, podcasts were made mainly by amateurs: teachers recording their lessons, fans discussing their favourite football team, or friends chatting about films. Equipment was cheap, and anyone with a microphone and a laptop could publish a programme. Traditional radio stations were slow to react. Many of them saw podcasts as a hobby rather than a threat, and it was several years before they began to offer their own programmes for download.

The real growth came with the smartphone. Once people could download and play episodes on a device they carried everywhere, listening became part of daily routines such as commuting, cooking and exercising. One survey of listeners in several countries found that more than half usually listened while doing something else. Perhaps surprisingly, the most common place to listen was at home, with the car in second place.

Podcasts differ from radio in several important ways. Because there is no schedule, an episode can be any length: some last ten minutes, others more than three hours. There are also far fewer rules about content. Presenters can explore a narrow subject in great depth, knowing that even a small audience scattered around the world may be enough to make the programme worthwhile. Many listeners say that podcasts feel more personal than radio, as if the presenter were talking directly to them.

Making money, however, has been a challenge. Most podcasts are free, so producers depend on advertising, which is usually read aloud by the presenter at the start or in the middle of an episode. Some ask listeners for voluntary donations, while a smaller number charge a monthly subscription for extra episodes. People who study the industry point out that only a small proportion of podcasts earn enough to pay their makers a full salary; for the majority, it remains a part-time activity.

Perhaps the most surprising development is the return of the long spoken story. Many successful podcasts are investigations that follow a single case over ten or twenty episodes, and some of these have been turned into television series. For an audience that is said to have a short attention span, listeners seem remarkably willing to spend hours with a good storyteller.

readings.title: Practice 2: Local news in the digital age
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 1 darajasi)
text: For most of the twentieth century, local newspapers were at the centre of community life. They reported on council meetings, school sports results and planning decisions, and they carried the advertisements through which people sold cars, rented flats and found jobs. In many towns, the local paper was also the only source of information about the courts and the police.

The internet changed this business very quickly. Classified advertisements, which had once provided a large part of a local paper's income, moved to free websites. At the same time, readers began to expect news to be free online. As a result, a great many local titles have closed or merged over the last two decades, and many of those that survive employ only a handful of reporters.

The effect has not been the same everywhere. Papers in large cities have often survived by building strong websites and attracting readers from outside their area, while those in small towns and rural districts have found it much harder. In some regions there is now no local reporter at all, a situation that journalists describe as a 'news desert'. Residents in such places may know more about events in the capital than about decisions taken by their own council.

Researchers have begun to study what happens when a town loses its newspaper. One study in the United States compared towns that had lost their paper with similar towns that had not. It found that in the first group, fewer people stood as candidates in local elections, and the cost of borrowing money for public projects rose. The researchers suggest that without reporters watching, local government becomes less efficient.

Not everyone agrees that the picture is so bleak. Social media groups now allow residents to share news about road closures, lost pets and local events within minutes, and some groups have more members than the local paper ever had readers. However, critics point out that such groups rarely check facts, and that rumours can spread as quickly as real news. Volunteers who run the groups are also unlikely to sit through a three-hour council meeting.

New models are appearing. Some local news sites are run as non-profit organisations and funded by donations from readers and grants from charitable foundations. Others ask readers to become members and pay a small monthly fee. A few towns have experimented with journalism students reporting on local affairs as part of their university course, supervised by experienced editors.

Whether any of these models can replace the traditional newspaper is still unclear. What is clear is that people value local news more than they are willing to pay for it: surveys regularly show that most residents think local journalism is important, but only a small minority have ever paid for it.

readings.title: Practice 3 (uyga): The digital detox
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 1 darajasi), uy vazifasi
text: A growing number of people are choosing to take a break from their phones, laptops and social media accounts. The practice, known as a 'digital detox', can last anything from a single evening to several weeks. Hotels in some countries now offer detox holidays, in which guests hand in their devices at reception on arrival and receive them back only when they leave.

The idea is not entirely new. For centuries, religious traditions have encouraged periods of silence and withdrawal from daily life, and some families have long kept mealtimes free of television. What is new is the scale of the habit that people are trying to break. Many adults now spend more of their waking hours looking at a screen than doing anything else, and for teenagers the figure is often higher still.

Supporters argue that constant connection has costs. Notifications interrupt concentration, and many people check their phones many times a day without really noticing. Using screens late in the evening has also been linked to poor sleep, partly because bright light from screens can delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy.

In one small experiment, researchers at a university asked a group of students to give up social media for a week, while a second group continued as normal. At the end of the week, the first group reported feeling less anxious and more satisfied with their lives. However, the effect was modest, and the researchers noted that the students knew the purpose of the study, which may have influenced their answers.

Critics of the detox movement make several points. First, many jobs now depend on being online, so a complete break is unrealistic for most workers. Second, the internet is where many people keep in touch with family and friends, especially those who live far away. Cutting this link, they argue, may increase loneliness rather than reduce it. Finally, a short break may achieve little if people simply return to their old habits afterwards.

For this reason, many psychologists now recommend small, permanent changes rather than dramatic breaks. Suggestions include switching off all non-essential notifications, keeping phones out of the bedroom, and choosing a fixed time in the evening after which screens are not used. Some people use apps that record how long they spend on each website, which can be a surprising experience. Others simply leave their phone in another room while they work or study, so that checking it requires a deliberate decision.

The irony, of course, is that much of the advice about disconnecting is found online. Even so, the popularity of the idea suggests that many people feel their relationship with technology needs to change.

intro: Section 4 — bitta ma'ruzachi akademik mavzuda gapiradi (ma'ruza, taqdimot). Oraliq tanaffus yo'q, shuning uchun tayyorlanish vaqtida 10 savolning HAMMASINI ko'rib chiqish kerak. Ma'ruzachi faqat fakt emas, fikr va maslahat ham beradi.

6.0 darajasida Section 4 ko'pincha ikki xil completion turidan iborat: gap (sentence) yoki summary completion va flow chart. Ikkalasida ham asosiy ish — bo'shliq GRAMMATIKASI: "a ___ or a video" — birlikdagi ot; "of little interest to a large ___" — ot; "earn money from ___" — ot yoki -ing.

Flow chart — jarayon bosqichlari, strelkalar bilan. Ma'ruzachi bosqichlarni signal so'zlar bilan ajratadi: "First of all", "Then", "Remember", "Once you've written...", "And another thing", "Finally". Signal so'zni eshitsangiz, keyingi qutiga o'ting.

Paraphrase: savoldagi so'z audioda boshqacha keladi. "Include ___ from people involved" = "put in quotations from people who are part of the story"; "check the accuracy of" = "make sure that ... are correct". Kalit so'zni emas, MA'NONI kuting.

TUZOQ: ma'ruzachi bir nechta mos keladigan so'zni aytadi. "Write a report ... take a photo ... make a video" — gapda "video" allaqachon bor, "a ___" — birlikdagi ot: photo. Workbook'da "web log" (1997) va "we blog" (1999) — savoldagi yilga qarang.

So'z chegarasi: Student's Book'da Q1–5 — ONE OR TWO WORDS, Q6–10 — ONE WORD ONLY. "quotations from people" — faqat "quotations". Imtihonda kitobda berilgan har ikki imlo ham qabul qilinadi (organisation / organization), lekin xato imlo — 0 ball.
Transfer: ko'plik -s, imlo va so'z soni. Flow chart'da kitob "quotes/quotations" ikkalasini qabul qiladi — lekin ikki variantni birga yozmang.
formulas: check the accuracy = make sure ... correct
presentation: Section 4 da tanaffus yo'q. Qachon o'qiyman?
Faqat boshidagi tayyorlanish vaqtida. Shuning uchun 1–10 ni bir yo'la ko'rib chiqing va so'z turini qalam bilan yozib qo'ying.
Flow chart'da qutilar tartibi o'zgarishi mumkinmi?
Deyarli yo'q: flow chart jarayon tartibida, audio ham shu tartibda.
Bo'shliqni o'tkazib yubordim. Nima qilaman?
Keyingi qutiga o'ting. Signal so'z eshitilsa, demak oldingi bosqich tugagan. Oxirida bo'sh qolganiga taxminiy so'z turini yozing.
Eshitgan so'zim bo'shliqqa grammatik mos kelmayapti.
Ehtimol noto'g'ri so'zni ushladingiz yoki ko'plik/birlik farq qiladi. Kitob maslahati: iloji bo'lsa eshitgan so'zingizni yozing.
"ONE WORD ONLY" da "a pyramid" deb yozsam-chi?
Artikl ham so'z hisoblanadi: "a" gapda allaqachon bor, faqat "pyramid".
Ma'ruzachi fikr bildirsa, bu ham javobmi?
Ha, Section 4 da ko'pincha shunday: "I think the main cause..." — fikr ham savol bo'lishi mumkin.
notes: 5.0 da sentence completion va flow chart'ni alohida o'rgangan edik. Endi ular bitta Section 4 ma'ruzasida, tanaffussiz ketma-ket keladi — asosiy ko'nikma: 10 bo'shliqni oldindan tayyorlash.
Tekshiruvda har javobdan keyin skriptdagi gapni ekranga chiqaring va signal so'zni boshqa rang bilan ko'rsating.
Kuchli o'quvchilarga: Workbook audiosini 1.25 tezlikda tinglash yoki Jony Academy skriptini o'quvchining o'zi sinfga o'qib berishi.

Birinchi nom so'ralgan; keyingi nom — tuzoq

how: CORE — maqola va blog yozish so'zlari; STRONG — ma'ruzada keladigan tavsif so'zlari; SUPER — og'zaki nutqdagi iboralar.
Har o'quvchi o'zi kuzatadigan bitta blog, kanal yoki sahifa haqida 3 gap aytadi, har gapda bitta yangi so'z.

class_ex.title: Bo'shliq turini oldindan aytish (SB, 2- va 4-mashq)
class_ex.instr: Tinglashdan oldin: har bo'shliqqa qanday so'z kerak — ot/fe'l/sifat, birlik yoki ko'plik?
items: 1 — "a news story, a ___ or a video"
2 — "of little interest to a large ___"
3 — "used to write a ___"
4 — "more likely to be a ___ rather than national"
5 — "earn money from ___"
6 — "in the shape of a ___"
7 — "Include ___ from people involved"
8 — "Check the accuracy of your ___"
9 — "Don't write a ___"
10 — "write an attractive ___"
why: "a ___ or a video" — video ga o'xshash narsa: artikl "a" — birlik.
"a large ___" — katta nima? Ko'p odamlar yoki tashkilot.
"write a ___" — yoziladigan narsa: xat, maqola.
"a ___ rather than national or international news" — mavzu turi.
"from ___" — daromad manbasi.
"the shape of a ___" — geometrik shakl.
"from people involved" — odamlardan olinadigan narsa, ko'plik.
"your ___" — tekshiriladigan narsalar: raqamlar, faktlar.
"a ___" — maqolaning qismi.
"an attractive ___" — maqolaning oxirida yoziladigan qismi (flow chart'da "Finally").
class_ex.note: "a" / "an" artikli — birlik belgisi. 10-savolda "an" "attractive" ga tegishli, javobning o'zi haqida hech narsa demaydi.

class_ex.title: Signal so'zlar: flow chart'ning qaysi qutisi?
class_ex.instr: Ustoz gapni o'qiydi. O'quvchilar: bu yangi bosqichmi, qaysi bosqich va qaysi so'z signal berdi?
items: "First of all, you need to decide how often you're going to post."
"Once you've written your article, go over it again."
"And another thing to bear in mind: people online stop reading quickly."
"Then check your statistics to see how many people are reading."
"Finally, you need to write a headline."
why: "First of all" — flow chart'ning birinchi qutisi.
"Once you've..." — oldingi bosqich tugaganini bildiradi.
"Another thing" — qo'shimcha qadam yoki maslahat.
"Then" — ketma-ketlik.
"Finally" — oxirgi quti. Bu so'zni eshitsangiz, oldingi bo'shliqlarga qaytmang.

tasks.type: Complete the sentences below. Write ONE OR TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: Gap tartibi = ma'ruza tartibi. Bo'shliq grammatikasini oldindan belgilang.
items: 1 Ordinary people can provide a news story, a ___ or a video when no professional journalist is present.
2 Amateur journalists often report on subjects which would be of little interest to a large ___.
3 In the past, someone who wanted to express an opinion used to write a ___, while now they write a blog.

why: "They can take a photo with a digital camera or use their mobile phone to make a video film". Tuzoq: "write a report" — bu "news story" ga to'g'ri keladi, u gapda allaqachon bor.

"One of the few ways of doing this was to send a letter to a newspaper". "Express an opinion" = "make your opinions known"; "blog" gapda bor.
"Amateur journalists often write about something which is a local issue". Keyin misollar: maktab, shahardagi tirbandlik.

tasks.type: Og'zaki
tasks.instr: Tinglashdan oldin Q6–10 ni ko'zdan kechiring.
items: Which three questions (6–10) need a noun to fill the gap?

tasks.title: Questions 1–5 — Blogs and the history of blogging
tasks.type: Complete the summary below. Write ONE OR TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: Summary ma'ruzaning birinchi yarmiga tegishli. Yillar (1994, 1999) — langar.
items: 1 Blogs are usually not ___ because they have interactive elements...
2 ...which may lead to friendships or even ___ relationships between people.
3 The first 'blog' was probably created in 1994 by a student and he called it his '___'.
4 Similar websites were then created and these included both links and ___.

why: "Most blogs are not monologues, because they allow readers to make their own comments". "Interactive elements" = o'quvchi izohlari.
"Perhaps making friends or even doing business with each other". "Friendships" summary'da bor.
"His site was called Justin's Home Page". Tuzoq: "he later called it Links From The Underground" — keyingi nom.
"With links to other websites and forums for people to contribute their personal opinions".
"In 1999, a blogger called Peter Merholz jokingly broke this word up into 'we blog'". Tuzoq: "web log" — 1997, Jorn Barger.

"Announce it by sending links to it on social networking sites". "Outstanding" = "particularly good ... really proud of".

Do some reading before starting a post.
As you compose the post, keep a record of (7) and links.
After creating the post, add some tags to it to improve searchability.
Use social networking sites to (8) a post you think is outstanding.

listenings.title: Jony Academy mashqi: Checking a news story before you share it
intro: Ma'ruza: onlayn yolg'on xabarlar va ularni tekshirish usuli. Ustoz tabiiy tezlikda, BIR MARTA o'qiydi; tayyorlanish uchun 45 soniya.
Ko'rsatma: Q1–5 — ONE OR TWO WORDS; Q6–10 — ONE WORD ONLY. Savollarni doskaga yoki varaqqa yozing.
transcript: LECTURER: Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about false information online — what people often call 'fake news'. In the first part I'll look at why it spreads so easily, and in the second part I'll give you a simple method for checking a story before you share it.

LECTURER: Let's start with a little history. False stories are nothing new. For centuries, rumours were passed from person to person, and later they appeared in printed leaflets and newspapers. What has changed is speed. Today, a false story on social media can reach millions of people in a single afternoon — long before anyone publishes a correction.

LECTURER: So why do people share these stories? You might expect the main reason to be that people want to trick others. In fact, research suggests that most people who share false information believe it is true. What matters is how a story makes us feel. Stories that cause strong emotions — especially anger or surprise — are shared far more often than calm, factual reports.

LECTURER: We are also much more likely to trust a story if it's passed on by a friend. And the effect is even stronger when it comes from a family member — even if that person has no idea where the story originally came from.

LECTURER: Pictures are another problem. A photograph can be completely genuine, but it may have been taken years earlier, or in a different country, and then presented as today's news. Many people assume that a photo is proof. It isn't.

LECTURER: Now, you might think that young people are better at spotting false stories, because they've grown up with the internet. Actually, studies of university students have found that many of them struggle to tell the difference between news and advertising — especially when an advert has been designed to look like an ordinary article.

LECTURER: So, how can you protect yourself? Here's a method I recommend. The first step is simply to stop. Don't share anything immediately, however exciting it seems. That pause is the most important part of the whole process.
LECTURER: Next, look at the source. Who actually published this story? If you don't recognise the website, find its 'About' page and see who runs it.
LECTURER: Then read beyond the headline. Headlines are written to attract clicks, and sometimes the article itself says something quite different — or much less dramatic.
LECTURER: After that, check the date. Old stories are often shared again as if they were new, particularly after a disaster or during an election.

LECTURER: The next step is to search for the same story on other websites. If something really important has happened, several reliable news organisations will be reporting it. If you can only find it in one place, be suspicious.

LECTURER: And finally, if the story includes a photo, do a reverse image search. This shows you where else the picture has appeared online, and when it was first published. If the story passes all these checks, then by all means share it. If it doesn't — the best thing you can do is nothing at all.

tasks.title: Questions 1–5
tasks.type: Complete the sentences below. Write ONE OR TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: Bo'shliq turini oldindan belgilang. Birinchi eshitgan mos so'zni darhol yozmang.
items: 1 A false story on social media can reach millions of people in a single ___.
2 Stories that cause strong ___ are shared more often than factual reports.
3 A story is trusted most when it is passed on by a ___.
4 A genuine photo may be misleading if it was taken years earlier or in a different ___.
5 Many university students find it hard to tell the difference between news and ___.
why: "A false story on social media can reach millions of people in a single afternoon". Tuzoq: "for centuries" — o'tmish haqida.
"Stories that cause strong emotions — especially anger or surprise — are shared far more often". "Anger" va "surprise" — misollar, bo'shliqqa umumiy so'z kerak.
"The effect is even stronger when it comes from a family member". Tuzoq: "a friend" birinchi eshitiladi, lekin savolda "most" — eng kuchli ta'sir.
"It may have been taken years earlier, or in a different country".
"Many of them struggle to tell the difference between news and advertising". Tuzoq: "young people are better" — ma'ruzachi buni rad etadi.
tasks.note: 3-savol — asosiy tuzoq: "friend" va "family member" ikkalasi ham eshitiladi. Savoldagi "most" ni doiraga oling.

tasks.title: Questions 6–10 — How to check a news story
tasks.type: Complete the flow chart below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.
tasks.instr: Signal so'zlar: The first step, Next, Then, After that, The next step, And finally.
why: "Next, look at the source. Who actually published this story?"
"Then read beyond the headline". "Read more than" = "read beyond".
"After that, check the date. Old stories are often shared again as if they were new".
"Search for the same story on other websites". Ko'plik -s — "other" dan keyin.
"Do a reverse image search". Bitta so'z: "search".
rows: Stop — don't share the story immediately.
Look at the (6) — who published the story?
Check the (8) to make sure the story is not old.
Look for the same story on other (9).
For photos, do a reverse image (10).

lessons.title: Mock test 1: Unit 1–4 dan keyin — to'liq imtihon va natijalar tahlili
lessons.grammar_topic: To'liq mockni o'tkazish (Listening 30, Reading 60, Writing 60 daqiqa — havola orqali kompyuterda) va natijani savol turlari bo'yicha Unit 1–4 ga bog'lab tahlil qilish
lessons.vocab_topic: Xom ball va band, olti xato sababi, savol turi bo'yicha naqsh, unitga qaytish, ikki haftalik reja
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy CRM mock bazasi — mock havolasi guruh test ekranidan ochiladi, Listening skriptini examiner ovoz chiqarib o'qiydi; examiner javoblar varaqasi har savol bo'yicha o'quvchining javobi, to'g'ri javob va mavzu belgisini ko'rsatadi; band rasmiy xom ball — band jadvali bo'yicha avtomatik qo'yiladi.
objectives: To'liq mockni tartib bilan o'tkazish: xona va ekran tayyorligi, qoidalar, Listening skriptini examiner o'qishi, tugatgan o'quvchi bilan ishlash.
To'liq qog'oz (30 + 60 + 60 = 150 daqiqa) bitta 120 daqiqalik darsga sig'masligini bilish: bu dars uning ramkasi.
O'z natijasini o'qish: xom ball, band va qaysi bo'lim o'rtachani pastga tortgani.
Har xato javobni olti sababdan bittasiga ajratish.
Xatolarni savol turi bo'yicha guruhlab, Unit 1–4 dagi qaysi darsga qaytish kerakligini aniqlash.
Maqsad bilan solishtirish (kamida 5.5: Listening 18+, Reading 19+ (40 dan)) va ikki haftalik aniq reja yozish.
materials: Chop etilgan ism ro'yxati: kim qaysi kompyuterda o'tirgani va kim tugatgani belgilanadi.
Ustoz ekranida examiner Listening skripti — faqat ustozda, o'quvchiga ko'rsatilmaydi.
Har stolda zaxira qog'oz va qalam: Listening paytida ism, raqam va sanalar qoralama qilinadi.
Doskada xona qoidalari va qolgan vaqt; tahlil qismida — Listening va Reading xom ball — band jadvallari.
Har o'quvchiga "Olti sabab" jadvali va "Savol turi → Unit" xaritasi (quyidagi 3-mashq jadvali) chop etilgan holda.
Har o'quvchiga "Ikki haftalik reja" varaqasi — 6 qator, oxirida ustoz imzosi uchun joy.
Proyektor: tahlilda examiner javoblar varaqasi guruh test ekrani orqali ochiladi.
timeline: Mock oldidan: xona va ekran tayyorligi
Kompyuterlar tekshiriladi, havola guruh test ekranidan ochiladi, examiner skripti ustoz ekranida, ism ro'yxati va zaxira qog'oz tarqatiladi.
Joylashtirish va xona qoidalari
Telefon sumkaga; sahifadan chiqish tizimda sanalishi ovoz chiqarib aytiladi; savol bo'lsa qo'l ko'tariladi.
Listeningni o'tkazish
Examiner Part 1–4 ni ovoz chiqarib BIR MARTA o'qiydi; skript faqat examiner ekranida.
Reading va Writing yurganda ustoz
Xona kuzatiladi, mazmun bo'yicha yordam berilmaydi, qolgan vaqt doskaga yozib boriladi.
Natijaning tushishi
Xom ball avtomatik bandga aylanib guruh jurnaliga tushadi; examiner javoblar varaqasi ochiladi.
Natijani ochish
Har o'quvchi xom ball va bandini daftariga yozadi va maqsad bilan solishtiradi (kamida 5.5: Listening 18+, Reading 19+ (40 dan)).
Xom ball — band jadvali
Doskada ikkala jadval; bitta savol yarim bandni o'zgartirishi ko'rsatiladi (2-mashq).
Olti sabab
Har sababga bitta tanish misol (1-mashq); sabablar jadvali tarqatiladi.
Javoblar varaqasi: Listening
Savol-savol o'qiladi, har xatoga sabab raqami va Section turi yoziladi.
Javoblar varaqasi: Reading
Passage bo'yicha ketma-ket; har xatoga sabab raqami va savol turi yoziladi.
Savol turi → Unit xaritasi
Xatolar savol turi bo'yicha guruhlanadi va Unit 1–4 dagi qaysi darsga qaytish kerakligi topiladi (3-mashq).
Ikki haftalik reja
Har kim eng katta ikki naqsh bo'yicha 6 qatorli reja yozadi; juftlik o'qib tekshiradi.
Xulosa va vazifa
Reja ustozga ko'rsatiladi va imzolanadi; xatolar daftari uyda to'ldiriladi.

intro: Bu dars ikki qismdan iborat: avval to'liq mock, keyin natijalarni savol-savol tahlil qilish. Yangi mavzu yo'q — bugun Unit 1–4 da o'rganilgan savol turlari kombinatsiyalari imtihon sharoitida o'lchanadi.

Mock havolasi guruh test ekranidan ochiladi, o'quvchilar kompyuterda ishlaydi. Listening 30, Reading 60, Writing 60 daqiqa — jami 150 daqiqa, ya'ni to'liq qog'oz bitta darsga sig'maydi: u shu slotdan tashqarida yoki ikki o'tirishda ishlanadi, bu dars esa uning ramkasi.
Listeningda yozuv qo'yilmaydi: skriptni EXAMINER ovoz chiqarib, bir marta va bir tekis tezlikda o'qiydi. Skript faqat examiner ekranida turadi.

Natija ikki raqam: XOM BALL (40 dan nechta) va BAND. Listening va Reading jadvallari bir xil emas: 26 ta to'g'ri javob Listeningda 6.5, Academic Readingda 6.0. Bitta savol ko'pincha yarim bandni o'zgartiradi — bo'sh javob qoldirmang.

Olti sabab: 1) eshitmadim / topa olmadim; 2) eshitdim, lekin xato yozdim (imlo, ko'plik, raqam); 3) vaqt yetmadi; 4) savol turini noto'g'ri tushundim (so'z limiti, NOT GIVEN va FALSE farqi, TWO letters); 5) taxmin qildim; 6) bilardim, lekin javobni o'zgartirdim.

6.0 ning yangiligi — tahlil SAVOL TURI bo'yicha. Har xatoning yonida savol turi yoziladi va "Savol turi → Unit" xaritasidan qaysi darsga qaytish kerakligi topiladi. Masalan, Matching headings da 3 ta xato — Unit 2 (3-dars) readinglari va Practice 1–3 qayta ishlanadi.
Kombinatsiya xatosini alohida belgilang: agar bir passage'da ikkinchi savol turiga vaqt yetmagan bo'lsa (3-sabab), muammo tur emas — xarita usuli va vaqt taqsimoti.
Maqsad: kamida 5.5: Listening 18+, Reading 19+ (40 dan). Maqsaddan past bo'lim — ikki haftalik rejaning birinchi qatori.
presentation: Mock nega kerak, darslar yetmaydimi?
Darsda har tur alohida ishlanadi; mockda hammasi aralash va vaqt bilan. Kombinatsiya ko'nikmasi faqat shu yerda o'lchanadi.
Ballim past chiqdi. Nima qilaman?
Avval sabablarni sanang. Ko'pincha 2-sabab (imlo, raqam) — bu eng tez tuzaladigan xato.
Xatolarim har xil turlarda. Qayerdan boshlayman?
Eng ko'p xato bo'lgan ikki turdan. Xaritadan ularning darsini toping.
Listening skriptini keyin berasizmi?
Yo'q. Tahlil faqat javoblar varaqasi orqali, skript o'quvchiga berilmaydi.
Vaqt yetmadi — bu qaysi sabab?
3-sabab. Davosi — xarita usuli va har passage uchun 20 daqiqa qoidasi (Unit 1).
Writingni ham tahlil qilamizmi?
Writing alohida baholanadi; bu darsning tahlili Listening va Readingga qaratilgan.
notes: Natijalarni ochishdan oldin o'quvchilarga eslating: mock — o'lchov, jazo emas. Maqsad — keyingi ikki haftada qaysi darsga qaytishni bilish.
Tahlil qismida ustoz ham guruh bo'yicha umumiy naqshni yozib oladi: agar guruhning yarmi bitta turda xato qilgan bo'lsa, o'sha unit keyingi haftada sinfda qayta ko'riladi.
Bu kurs o'rtasidagi mock: natija Unit 5–8 ni boshlashdan oldin qaysi turlarni mustahkamlash kerakligini ko'rsatadi.

lessons.title: Unit 5 Reading — Passage 2: Matching information + Matching features + Summary completion
lessons.grammar_topic: Uch savol turi bitta passage'da: Matching information + Matching features + Summary completion (Passage 2)
lessons.vocab_topic: Unit 5 (The world in our hands) — qayta tiklanadigan energiya, iqlim o'zgarishi, tabiatni asrash
lessons.book_ref: Complete IELTS Bands 5–6.5: Student's Book, Unit 5, 50–52-betlar (Reading Section 2); Workbook, Unit 5, 32–33-betlar. Practice 1–3 — Jony Academy matnlari.
objectives: Passage 2 da uch savol turi kelganda ishlash tartibini tanlash: avval tartibli tur (summary), keyin ismlar (matching features), oxirida matching information.
Matching information savolidagi birinchi so'zlardan ma'lumot TURINI aniqlash (estimate, comparison, suggestion, description) va xatboshidan aynan shu turdagi gapni topish.
Matching features uchun matndagi barcha ism va tashkilotlarni 2 daqiqada doiraga olib, har birining yoniga 2–3 so'zli izoh yozish.
Tuzoqni tanish: bitta xatboshida ikki tashkilot yoki bir xil raqam (2020) tilga olinsa, fikr aynan kimniki ekanini tekshirish.
Summary sarlavhasidan kerakli xatboshini topish va javobni so'z chegarasi (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS) hamda so'z turiga mos ko'chirish.
materials: Student's Book, Unit 5, 50–52-betlar ("Out of Africa: solar energy from the Sahara") — sinfda birga ishlanadi.
Workbook, Unit 5, 32–33-betlar ("Russia's boreal forests and wild grasses could combat climate change") — mustaqil mashq.
Practice 1–3 matnlari chop etilgan varaqlar (har o'quvchiga) — pastdagi Reading bo'limidan.
Rangli qalamlar: ism/tashkilotlar — doira, matching information kalit g'oyasi — to'lqinli chiziq.
Doskada uch ustun: "Summary → qaysi xatbosh?", "Ismlar → qaysi xatboshilar?", "Information → ma'lumot turi".

Uch tur — bitta passage
Ustoz doskada: ishlash tartibi, har tur qoidasi, NEVER va USUALLY guruhlari, tuzoqlar.
Sinf mashqi

intro: Passage 2 da 6.0 darajasida ko'pincha uch savol turi birga keladi. Student's Book'dagi Sahara matnida: 1–5 Matching information (qaysi xatboshida?), 6–9 Matching features (qaysi tashkilot?), 10–13 Summary completion (matndan ikki so'zgacha). Workbook'da ham aynan shu uchlik.

Muammo: uch turning ikkitasi NEVER guruhida — matching information va matching features savollari matn tartibida kelmaydi. Faqat summary odatda (USUALLY) tartibli va bitta-ikkita xatboshiga tegishli. Shuning uchun navbatni o'zgartiramiz.

TAVSIYA ETILGAN TARTIB: 1) sarlavha va kichik sarlavha — 30 soniya; 2) SUMMARY — sarlavhasi ("Concentrating Solar Power") kerakli xatboshini ko'rsatadi, uni o'qib 4 javobni yozasiz; 3) MATCHING FEATURES — matndagi barcha ism/tashkilotlarni doiraga olasiz (ular ro'yxatda matn tartibida berilgan!) va gaplarni solishtirasiz; 4) MATCHING INFORMATION — endi matn tanish, eng oxirida ishlanadi.

Matching features: ro'yxatdagi variantlar ko'pincha savollardan ko'p (7 ta tashkilot — 4 ta savol). Ro'yxat tartibi = matn tartibi, bu xarita uchun juda qulay. Har ism yoniga 2–3 so'z yozing: "Abengoa — building 2 plants", "e-Parliament — start small".

Matching information: savolning boshidagi so'zlar ma'lumot TURINI aytadi — "estimates of" (raqam, hisob), "a comparison of" (ikki narsa solishtiriladi), "a suggestion for" (maslahat), "a mention of" (qisqa eslatma), "a short description of" (tasvir). Xatboshining asosiy g'oyasini emas, ichidagi bitta detalni qidirasiz (5.0 dagi headings bilan farqini eslang).

Uch tur bir-biriga yordam beradi: summary uchun o'qigan xatboshi, ismlar uchun chizgan xaritangiz — matching information uchun tayyor bilim. Oxirida 1–5 savollarning ko'pchiligini xotiradan joylashtirasiz, faqat tekshirish uchun qaytib o'qiysiz.
Vaqt: Passage 2 ga 20 daqiqa. Taxminan: summary — 5, matching features — 6, matching information — 7, tekshiruv — 2 daqiqa.
formulas: E ikki marta? NB ruxsat beradi
presentation: Nega 1–5 ni oxirida ishlaymiz?
Chunki ular tartibsiz va butun matnni qamraydi. Summary va ismlardan keyin matn allaqachon tanish bo'ladi.
Ro'yxatda 7 ta tashkilot, savol 4 ta. Qolganlari nima?
Ortiqcha variantlar — tuzoq. Ular matnda bor, lekin hech bir gapga mos kelmaydi.
Bitta xatboshida ikki tashkilot bor. Qanday ajrataman?
Fe'lga va egaga qarang: kim quryapti, kim qonun qabul qilgan, kim hisoblagan? Gap aynan kimga tegishli?
"NB You may use any letter more than once" nima degani?
Bitta xatbosh (masalan, E) ikki savolga javob bo'lishi mumkin. Ikki marta chiqsa, xato deb o'ylamang.
Summary'dagi so'z matndagidan boshqacha.
Normal: summary paraphrase qiladi ("situated in" = "building ... in"). Javob esa matndagi so'z, aynan o'sha shaklda.
Summary javobi uch so'z chiqdi.
Chegarani buzmang: kerakli ot odatda bitta so'z ("depressions"), ortiqcha sifat va artikl tashlanadi.
notes: 5.0 da matching information (25-dars), matching features (26-dars) va summary (14-dars) alohida o'rganilgan. Bugungi yangilik — uchalasini bitta passage'da, to'g'ri NAVBAT bilan yechish.
Tekshiruvda har javob uchun o'quvchidan ikki narsa so'rang: "isbot gap qaysi?" va "savoldagi qaysi so'z matnda qanday aytilgan?"
Kuchli o'quvchilarga: SB matnidagi 7 tashkilotning har biri haqida bir gapli izohni xotiradan aytish; zaif o'quvchilarga — faqat ism va xatboshi harfi.
mistakes: Matching information'ni birinchi ishlash va har savolga butun matnni o'qish
Tashkilot nomi yonidagi gapni o'ylamay tanlash (6-savolda DESERTEC — "by 2020")
Bitta harf ikki marta chiqqani uchun javobni o'zgartirish

how: CORE — energiya va ekologiya mavzusidagi asosiy so'zlar; STRONG — Passage 2 dagi akademik fe'l va otlar; SUPER — maqola uslubidagi iboralar.

readings.title: Practice 1: Power from the sea
readings.qtype: Matching information (1–5) + Matching features (6–9) + Summary completion (10–13)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 2 darajasi); ismlar o'quv maqsadida to'qilgan
text: A  When the world's first offshore wind farm was switched on off the coast of Denmark in 1991, it consisted of just eleven small turbines, and many engineers regarded it as an expensive experiment. Three decades later, wind farms at sea supply a significant share of the electricity used in several northern European countries, and the largest turbines now stand taller than most city office buildings. A single turn of their enormous blades can produce enough electricity to run an ordinary home for many hours.

B  The main attraction of building at sea is the wind itself. Out on the open water there are no hills, trees or buildings to slow the air down, so winds are both stronger and more constant than on land. In addition, turbines placed far from the coast are rarely seen or heard by anyone, which removes one of the most common objections to wind power. 'On land, the biggest obstacle is usually not engineering but neighbours,' says Marta Lind, an engineer who has worked on several North Sea projects. 'At sea, the difficulties are technical, and technical problems can be solved.'

C  Those difficulties are considerable. Most offshore turbines stand on foundations made of steel or concrete and fixed to the seabed, which is only practical in water less than about fifty metres deep. For deeper seas, engineers have developed floating turbines. Instead of resting on the bottom, each turbine is mounted on a large platform that is partly filled with water to keep it stable, and the platform is held in position by cables attached to heavy anchors on the seabed. The electricity then travels to the shore through cables buried beneath the sea floor.

D  Environmental groups have generally welcomed offshore wind, but not without reservations. Seabirds can be killed by the blades, and the noise of hammering foundations into the seabed may disturb whales and dolphins. Marine biologist Tomas Reyes, however, points to an unexpected benefit. 'Within a few years the foundations are covered in mussels and seaweed, and fish gather around them,' he explains. 'In effect, a wind farm can become an artificial reef.' He adds that because fishing boats usually stay out of these areas, some fish populations have a chance to recover.

E  Not everyone sees that as good news. Fishing communities complain that wind farms close traditional fishing grounds and that they are rarely consulted before a site is chosen. Peter Holm, who represents a group of small fishing businesses, says the turbines themselves are not the problem. 'We are not against clean energy,' he says. 'We simply want to be involved from the start, instead of being told about a project when all the decisions have already been made.'

F  Cost has long been the main argument against offshore wind. Building and maintaining machines in salt water and storms is far more expensive than doing so on land. Yet prices have fallen sharply over the past decade as turbines have grown larger and construction methods have improved. Government adviser Sara Novak believes the industry has reached a turning point. 'Ten years ago, electricity from offshore wind cost much more than power from gas,' she says. 'In many places today the difference has almost disappeared.'

G  The greatest remaining challenge may be what happens when the wind drops or suddenly becomes much stronger. Existing electricity networks were designed for power stations that produce a steady supply, and they cannot always absorb sudden surges from the sea. Engineers are therefore testing ways of storing surplus energy, for example by using it to produce hydrogen, which can be kept and burned later. Marta Lind is optimistic. In her view, within twenty years the question will not be whether offshore wind can meet a country's needs, but how quickly the networks can be rebuilt to carry it.
