readings.title: Practice 2: Bringing back the beaver
readings.qtype: Matching information (1–5) + Matching features (6–9) + Summary completion (10–13)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 2 darajasi); ismlar o'quv maqsadida to'qilgan
text: A  Beavers were once common in rivers across Europe and northern Asia. Over the centuries, however, they were hunted in huge numbers, partly for their thick fur and partly for a strong-smelling substance they produce, which was used in medicines and perfumes. By the early twentieth century only small groups survived in a few isolated areas. Since then, protection and reintroduction programmes have been remarkably successful, and the number of beavers in Europe is now thought to be well over a million. In Britain, where the animal had disappeared several hundred years earlier, the first officially approved release into the wild did not take place until the early twenty-first century.

B  Few animals change their surroundings as dramatically as beavers do. Using their powerful teeth, they cut down young trees and use the branches, together with stones and mud, to build dams across streams. Water collects behind each dam and forms a pond. In the middle of this pond the beavers construct their home, known as a lodge. Its entrances are always underwater, which makes it very difficult for predators such as wolves to get inside.

C  For people living downstream, these dams can bring real benefits. During heavy rain, the ponds hold back large quantities of water and release it slowly over several days, reducing the risk of sudden floods. 'A series of beaver dams works rather like a sponge,' explains hydrologist Emma Clarke. 'It will not prevent every flood, but it can reduce the peak flow that reaches the towns further down the valley, and that is often where the most expensive damage happens.' Beaver ponds also trap soil and pollution, so the water that leaves them tends to be cleaner.

D  The ponds are equally valuable for wildlife. Dead trees standing in the water attract insects and woodpeckers, while the still, shallow edges are ideal for frogs, dragonflies and water birds. Ecologist James Ward has studied several sites where beavers were released. 'Within five years, the variety of species at some of them had increased dramatically,' he says. 'The ponds act as nurseries, where young fish and frogs can grow without being carried away by fast-moving water.'

E  Not everyone is pleased to see the animals return, however. Farmers complain that dams can flood valuable fields and block drainage ditches, and that beavers sometimes damage fruit trees. In some regions, landowners can now receive compensation for these losses. Farmer Tom Baxter, whose land lies beside a river where beavers have settled, accepts that they have a place in the countryside. 'My problem is the paperwork,' he says. 'When a dam floods my field, I need permission to remove it within days, not months.'

F  Managing these conflicts is now a major part of conservation work. In several countries, beavers that cause serious problems can be caught and moved to more suitable rivers, and in some places simple pipes are fitted through dams to keep water at a safe level. Other measures are even more basic: wire fences can be placed around individual trees that owners want to protect, and some landowners simply accept a small amount of damage as the price of a healthier river. Conservation officer Nadia Rossi believes that the most effective tool is knowledge. 'Many of the fears people have come from stories rather than facts,' she says. 'When landowners understand how beavers behave, they are far more willing to share the river with them.'

readings.title: Practice 3 (uyga): Gardens on the roof
readings.qtype: Matching information (1–5) + Matching features (6–9) + Summary completion (10–13)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 2 darajasi), uy vazifasi; ismlar o'quv maqsadida to'qilgan
text: A  Covering a roof with plants is not a new idea. In Scandinavia, farmhouses have been built with roofs of grass and earth for centuries, because the thick layer helped to keep homes warm through long winters. The modern green roof, however, is a much more technical product. It was developed largely in Germany in the second half of the twentieth century, and today green roofs can be seen on offices, schools, shopping centres and even bus shelters in cities around the world.

B  A modern green roof is built in layers. At the bottom is a waterproof membrane that stops water from entering the building. Above this lies a root barrier, which prevents plant roots from growing into the roof and damaging it. Next comes a drainage layer that allows extra water to run away, and on top of that a growing medium, which is much lighter than ordinary garden soil. Most roofs are planted with low-growing species such as sedum, which can survive long periods of dry weather and need very little care.

C  One of the main reasons cities are interested in green roofs is rain. In a typical city, most surfaces are hard, so rainwater runs straight into the drains, which can quickly become overloaded during a storm. A green roof acts differently: the plants and growing medium absorb a large part of the rain and release it slowly, partly through evaporation. 'We used to think of drains and roofs as completely separate problems,' says urban planner Leila Haddad. 'In fact, every roof is part of a city's water system, and it should be planned that way.'

D  Green roofs also affect temperature. Cities are usually several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, especially at night, because concrete and asphalt store heat. Plants cool the air around them, and the layers of a green roof protect the building below from the summer sun. Building engineer Oliver Grant points out, however, that the benefit is not spread evenly. 'The rooms directly under the roof gain the most,' he says. 'In a tall building, people on the lower floors may notice very little difference.'

E  For wildlife, a green roof can be a small island in a desert of concrete. Bees, butterflies and beetles quickly find these spaces, and some birds use them for feeding and even nesting. Ecologist Ana Sousa warns that not all green roofs are equally useful. 'A roof covered with a single type of plant looks neat, but it offers food for very few species,' she explains. 'If we want real variety, we need different plants, some deeper soil and even a few stones or pieces of dead wood.'

F  Despite these advantages, green roofs remain relatively uncommon. They cost more to install than conventional roofs, and a roof full of wet soil is heavy, so many older buildings would need to be strengthened before one could be added. Property developer Ben Carter admits that price is the main obstacle. 'Most builders know green roofs are a good idea,' he says. 'But when a client compares the first bill, the ordinary roof usually wins, even if the green one saves money over thirty years.'

G  To change this situation, a number of cities now require green roofs on certain types of new building, while others offer grants or lower taxes to owners who install them. Some also allow developers to build slightly larger buildings if they include a planted roof. Supporters hope that these measures will make green roofs as ordinary as solar panels, turning thousands of empty grey surfaces into living spaces.

intro: Section 1 — kundalik suhbat (sayohat agentligi, ko'ngillilar tashkiloti, ro'yxatdan o'tish). 6.0 darajasida bu yerda ko'pincha ikki xil "completion" keladi: avval notes (qisqa yozuvlar), keyin table (jadval). Ikkalasi ham bo'shliq to'ldirish, lekin o'qish usuli boshqa.

ENG MUHIM FARQ — so'z chegarasi. Student's Book'da Q1–6: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER, Q7–10: ONE OR TWO WORDS. Workbook'da Q1–6: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER, Q7–10: ONE WORD. Har guruh ko'rsatmasini alohida o'qing va ramkaga oling — ikkinchi guruhda ko'pchilik birinchisining qoidasi bilan yozib, ball yo'qotadi.

NOTES: gaplar to'liq emas ("Will pay up to £ ___", "Needs quote for ___ during holiday"). Bo'shliq atrofidagi so'z turi aytadi: £ dan keyin — raqam; "for" dan keyin — ot; "a ___" — birlikdagi ot. Notes'da bor so'zni (£, "on plane") javobga qo'shmang.

TABLE: avval jadval sarlavhasi va ustun nomlarini o'qing (type of holiday / accommodation / advantage). Suhbat odatda QATOR bo'yicha boradi: bitta joy haqida uchala ustun, keyin keyingi joy. Qatordagi tayyor katakchalar ("watching animals", "village house") — qayerda turganingizni bildiruvchi "belgi".

TUZOQLAR: 1) tuzatish — "I originally planned three weeks, but actually two would be better" → oxirgi javob; 2) yaqin raqamlar — "over 300 groups and around 150,000 members" → jadvalda "300 ___" — demak "groups"; 3) sinonim — notes'da "paid staff", audioda avval "salaried people", keyin "paid staff".
Transfer: raqam — son bilan va vergul bilan (1,750; 130,000); ko'plik -s (cyclists, fences); imlo (vegetarian, insurance). Nom bosh harf bilan (City Farms, Action).
formulas: Table: ustun va qator nomlarini o'qing
presentation: Notes'da "£" bor. Men ham yozamanmi?
Yo'q. Faqat raqam: 1,750. Belgi allaqachon berilgan.
"ONE OR TWO WORDS" va "ONE WORD" farqi katta-mi?
Ha. "local family" birinchisida to'g'ri, ikkinchisida xato bo'ladi. Har guruh ko'rsatmasini qayta o'qing.
Jadvalda qatorlar tartibi buzilishi mumkinmi?
Odatda yo'q: agent joylarni jadval tartibida aytadi. Lekin bitta qator ichida ustunlar aralash kelishi mumkin.
Raqam jadvalda allaqachon bor (300 ___). Nima yozaman?
Raqamdan keyingi otni: "300 groups". 150,000 — boshqa narsa (a'zolar) soni.
Gapiruvchi o'z fikrini o'zgartirdi.
Oxirgi, tasdiqlangan javobni yozing: "originally ... but actually" dan keyingisi.
Q6 bilan Q7 orasida pauza bo'ladimi?
Student's Book'da ha — ikki alohida track. Workbook'da pauza bor; shu vaqtda jadval ustunlarini o'qing.
notes: 5.0 da note completion (5-dars) va table completion (16-dars) alohida o'rganilgan. Bugun ular bitta section'da ketma-ket keladi va har birining so'z chegarasi boshqa — asosiy ko'nikma shu.
Tekshiruvda har javobdan keyin skriptdagi gapni ekranga chiqaring; tuzatish va chalg'ituvchi raqamni boshqa rang bilan belgilang.
Kuchli o'quvchilarga: Workbook audiosini skriptsiz ikkinchi marta tinglab, har tashkilot haqida bitta qo'shimcha faktni yozish (branches soni, members soni).

class_ex.title: Bo'shliq turini bashorat qilish (SB, 2- va 4-mashq)
class_ex.instr: Audioni tinglashdan oldin SB Q1–10 dagi har bo'shliqqa qanday ma'lumot kerakligini ayting.
items: 1 Length of holiday: ___
2 Will pay up to £ ___
3 Told him about ___ for advance payments
4 Needs quote for ___ during holiday
5 Requires ___ on plane
6 Must check if he needs a ___
7 accommodation: house in a ___
8 type of holiday: live with a ___
9 type of holiday: working in a ___
10 advantage: holiday location without ___
why: "Length" — qancha vaqt: kun, hafta, oy.
£ belgisi turibdi — faqat raqam yoziladi.
"for advance payments" — oldindan to'lov uchun beriladigan narsa.
"quote" — narx taklifi; sayohat paytida kerak bo'ladigan xizmat.
"on plane" — parvozdagi maxsus talab.
"a ___" — birlikdagi ot; sayohatdan oldin tekshiriladigan narsa.
"house in a" — uy qayerda joylashgan?
"live with a" — kim bilan yashaydi?
"working in a" — qayerda ishlaydi?
"without" — ko'pincha salbiy narsa: mashinalar, turistlar, shovqin.
class_ex.note: Bashoratlarni doskada qoldiring; tinglashdan keyin qaysilari to'g'ri chiqqanini belgilang. Q7–10 chegarasi (ONE OR TWO WORDS) Q1–6 dan farq qilishini alohida ta'kidlang.

class_ex.title: "Oxirgi javob" — tuzoq mashqi
class_ex.instr: Ustoz gapni o'qiydi. O'quvchilar javobni aytadi va tuzoqni ko'rsatadi.
items: "We booked ten nights at first, but in the end we only stayed a week." — Length of stay?
"Rooms cost from 40 dollars, but I'd rather not spend more than 65 a night." — Maximum price?
"There are 12 branches and about 9,000 members in 400 teams." — Table: 400 ___
"You'll paint walls, but most of the time you'll be building bridges over streams." — Main activity: building ___
"There are no shops nearby, which some people don't like, but the best thing is that there's no traffic at all." — Advantage: a place without ___ (ONE WORD)
why: "At first ... but in the end" — tuzatishdan keyingi javob.
40 — eng past narx; savol eng ko'p to'lovni so'raydi.
400 raqamidan keyin kelgan ot — "teams". 9,000 — a'zolar soni, tuzoq.
"Most of the time" — asosiy faoliyat. "Walls" — qo'shimcha.
"Advantage" — afzallik: "the best thing" signal. Do'kon yo'qligi "some people don't like" — kamchilik, tuzoq.
class_ex.note: 5-gap SB Q10 ga tayyorgarlik: jadval ustuni (advantage) qaysi "without" kerakligini ko'rsatadi.

listenings.title: Jony Academy: Green Weekend — volunteer registration (Q1–10)
intro: Dilnoza shahar "Green Weekend" tadbiriga guruhini ro'yxatdan o'tkazish uchun qo'ng'iroq qiladi. Ustoz skriptni BIR MARTA, tabiiy tezlikda o'qiydi (ikki rol).

transcript: ORGANISER: Good morning, Green Weekend office. How can I help you?
DILNOZA: Hello. I'd like to register a group of volunteers for this weekend, please.
ORGANISER: Of course. Can I have your name?
DILNOZA: Yes, it's Dilnoza Karimova. That's K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A.
ORGANISER: K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A. Thank you. And how many people are in your group?
DILNOZA: Well, there were eight of us, but two of my friends have exams on Saturday, so it'll be six.

ORGANISER: Six, fine. Now, everyone meets on Saturday morning. Usually we meet at the main entrance of the park, but it's being repaired at the moment, so this time we're meeting in the car park next to the sports centre.
DILNOZA: Next to the sports centre. OK. Do we need to bring anything? Gloves?
ORGANISER: No, we provide gloves and rubbish bags for everyone. But please bring strong boots, because the river bank can be very muddy. And a water bottle, of course.
DILNOZA: Boots and a water bottle. And when do I need to confirm the names?
ORGANISER: Registration closes on Thursday. I know the website says Friday, but that's a mistake — we need the list a day earlier to order the equipment.
DILNOZA: Thursday, then. Could you tell me what activities there are?

ORGANISER: Sure. There are four. The biggest one is the river clean-up on the north bank. People expect to find leaves and branches, but most of what we pull out of the water is plastic — bottles, bags, that sort of thing.
DILNOZA: That's sad. What else?

ORGANISER: Then there's tree planting. That happens on the grass near the bridge — not the old footbridge, the new road bridge. Last year we planted two hundred trees, and our long-term aim is five hundred, but this weekend we've got 150 young trees ready.
DILNOZA: 150. My younger brother might like that. Is there anything for children?
ORGANISER: Yes, the bird box workshop in the community centre. It used to be for children over six, but the tools are quite sharp, so now it's only for children over eight.
DILNOZA: He's nine, so that's perfect. And the fourth activity?

ORGANISER: The litter survey in the town centre. Volunteers count and record the rubbish they find in each street, and all the results go to the local council, so they can decide where to put new bins.

intro: Bu darsda bitta Passage 1 da UCH savol turi keladi: chizma (diagram labelling), TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN va flow chart. Uch tur — uch xil o'qish usuli, shuning uchun boshlashdan oldin 1–2 daqiqa xarita tuzish shart.

Chizma va flow chart — "mahalliy" savollar: ular matnning bitta yoki ikki-uch xatboshisiga tegishli. Sarlavhani o'qing: "Layout of typical supermarket" — do'kon ichidagi joylar tasvirlangan xatboshilar; "In-store bread production process" — faqat non haqidagi bitta xatbosh. Butun matnni qayta o'qish shart emas.
T/F/NG — "tarqoq" savollar: ular butun matn bo'ylab tartib bilan keladi. Har savoldan kalit so'zni belgilang (ism, noyob so'z: greeters, bakeries, right-handed, decoy) va matndan skanerlab toping.

Chizmada javoblar matn tartibida KELMASLIGI mumkin — chizmadagi joylashuv bo'yicha raqamlanadi. Berilgan yorliqlar (pharmacy, milk, WAY IN) sizga yo'l ko'rsatadi: ular matnda qayerda tilga olingan bo'lsa, yonidagi bo'shliq javobi ham o'sha yerda.

Flow chart esa jarayon — bosqichlar deyarli har doim matn tartibida boradi. Strelkalar "keyin nima bo'ldi?" degan savolga javob beradi. Bo'shliq atrofidagi so'zlardan so'z turini aniqlang: "is sent ___ and other items" — ko'plikdagi ot.
So'z chegarasi har guruhda boshqacha bo'lishi mumkin: SB da chizma — NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS, flow chart — NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS. Har guruh ko'rsatmasini alohida o'qing va chegarani doiraga oling.
Tavsiya etilgan tartib: 1) uchala ko'rsatma va sarlavhalar (1–2 daqiqa); 2) chizma; 3) T/F/NG; 4) flow chart. Qiyin savolda 2 daqiqadan ortiq to'xtamang — belgilab, keyingisiga o'ting.
formulas: Layout of typical supermarket; milk, pharmacy
presentation: Qaysi guruhdan boshlayman?
Odatda raqam tartibida. Lekin chizma va flow chart'ning qaysi xatboshiga tegishli ekanini boshidayoq belgilab qo'ying — T/F/NG ni o'qiyotganda o'sha joylarga ham ko'zingiz tushadi.
Chizmadagi javoblar ham tartibdami?
Har doim emas. Chizma joylashuv bo'yicha raqamlanadi. Berilgan yorliqlarni matndan topib, atrofini o'qing.
Flow chart'dagi javoblar-chi?
Deyarli har doim tartibda — jarayon matnda qanday tasvirlangan bo'lsa, shunday.
Savoldagi solishtirish matnda yo'q bo'lsa?
"Wider range than...", "easier to persuade than..." — agar matn bu ikki narsani solishtirmasa, javob NOT GIVEN.
"is said to cut shoplifting" va "increase sales" — bir xilmi?
Yo'q. O'g'irlikni kamaytirish va savdoni oshirish — boshqa-boshqa da'vo. Savdo haqida gap yo'q — NOT GIVEN.
Javobni o'z so'zim bilan yozsam bo'ladimi?
Yo'q. Chizma va flow chart'ga faqat matndagi so'z, aynan o'sha shaklda yoziladi.
notes: Bu darsning yangiligi — bitta passage'da UCH tur. 5.0 da chizma (7-dars) va flow chart (4-dars) alohida o'rganilgan; endi ularni T/F/NG bilan bitta 20 daqiqada birga yechamiz.
Har javobdan keyin ikki savol bering: "isbot qaysi gapda?" va "savoldagi qaysi so'z matnda qanday aytilgan?"
Kuchli o'quvchilarga: SB matnini o'qimasdan, faqat uch sarlavha va yorliqlarga qarab, qaysi savol qaysi xatboshida ekanini 2 daqiqada taxmin qilish, keyin tekshirish.
Eslatma: 30-Day Reading Challenge'dagi Day 7 va Day 10 — aynan shu darsdagi SB va WB matnlari. Ularni uyga bermang, boshqa "Day" lardan foydalaning.

readings.title: Practice 1: Why shopping centres look the way they do
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn va chizma (Passage 1 darajasi)
text: Most people visit a shopping centre with a short list of things to buy, yet many leave with bags full of items they never planned to purchase. This is rarely an accident. The layout of a modern shopping centre is carefully planned by architects and retail consultants, and almost every feature is intended to keep visitors walking, looking and spending for as long as possible.

The most important decision concerns the position of the largest shops, which are known in the industry as 'anchor stores'. These are usually department stores or large supermarkets that attract customers on their own. Designers normally place one anchor store at each end of the building, so that people who want to go from one to the other must pass dozens of smaller shops on the way. This arrangement is sometimes called the 'dumbbell' layout, because the plan looks like the piece of gym equipment, with a heavy weight at both ends and a long bar in between.

The main walkway between the anchors is rarely straight. Gentle curves mean that shoppers can never see more than a few shop fronts ahead, which encourages them to keep going to find out what comes next. Benches are placed in the middle of the walkway rather than against the walls, so that people who sit down are still facing the shop windows. Some designers also use different floor materials: hard, shiny floors in the walkway keep people moving, while softer surfaces just outside shop doors invite them to slow down and look inside.

Moving between floors is also controlled. In many centres the escalators are not placed one above the other. Instead, a shopper who arrives on the first floor has to walk some distance to reach the next escalator, passing more shops as they do so. Lifts, which are needed by parents with pushchairs and people in wheelchairs, are often located near the entrances, where they are easy to find but do not interrupt the flow of shoppers.

The food court is almost always on the top floor. Hungry visitors must travel through the whole building to reach it, and after eating they tend to take the escalators back down, passing through the shopping floors once again. Toilets are frequently placed next to the food court for the same reason.

Light and sound matter too. Many shopping centres have glass roofs, because natural daylight makes people feel relaxed. However, there are very few clocks and, on the lower floors, very few windows looking outside, which makes it easy to lose track of time. Some critics argue that these techniques are manipulative, but developers reply that they simply create a comfortable place in which people want to stay. Background music is usually kept quiet and slow, since fast music tends to make people hurry, and pleasant smells from cafés and bakeries are often allowed to spread into the walkways.

readings.title: Practice 2: The cash machine
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn va chizma (Passage 1 darajasi)
text: Today it is hard to imagine life without cash machines, but they are a relatively recent invention. The machine usually described as the first working cash machine was opened by a bank in north London in 1967. It did not use plastic cards. Instead, customers obtained special paper vouchers from the bank, which they fed into the machine together with a personal number. The machine then gave out a fixed amount of money.

The personal number, now known as a PIN, was originally planned to be six digits long. According to a popular story, the inventor reduced it to four after his wife said that four numbers were the most she could easily remember. Four-digit PINs are still the most common today, although some countries use longer ones. In most systems, the card is blocked if the wrong PIN is entered three times in a row.

A modern cash machine looks simple from the outside, but its front panel contains several separate parts. At the top is a screen that shows instructions, and in many machines there are buttons on either side of it for choosing options. Next to the keypad is the card slot. Most keypads now have a small raised dot on the number 5, which helps blind users find the keys by touch. The cash comes out of a narrow opening called the dispenser, usually located below the keypad, while a separate slot to the side prints receipts. Many machines also have a small camera above the screen, which records each customer for security reasons.

Inside, the machine is connected to the bank's central computer. When a customer asks for money, the whole process takes only a few seconds. First, the machine reads the information stored on the card's chip or magnetic strip. The customer then enters their PIN, which is checked by the bank's central computer rather than by the machine itself. Next, the computer checks whether there is enough money in the account. If there is, it sends a message back to the machine, which counts the notes. Finally, the card is returned — in most modern machines before the cash is released, because experience showed that people often forgot their cards once they had their money.

Although cash payments are falling in many countries as more people pay by card or phone, cash machines are still used millions of times every day. Some banks have even added new functions, allowing customers to pay in cash, pay bills or top up their mobile phones. At the same time, criminals sometimes attach false devices to the card slot in order to copy card details, so banks advise customers to check the machine and to cover the keypad with their hand when typing their PIN.

readings.title: Practice 3 (uyga): How coins are made
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn va chizma (Passage 1 darajasi), uy vazifasi
text: Although more and more payments are made electronically, coins are still produced in huge numbers. National mints — the organisations that make a country's coins — produce billions every year, partly to replace old coins and partly because people keep coins at home in jars and drawers, where they are effectively lost to the economy. In some countries, producing the smallest coins actually costs more than the coins are worth.

Each coin has several parts. The side with the main design, often a portrait of a head of state or a national symbol, is called the 'obverse', or 'heads'. The other side, the 'reverse', or 'tails', usually shows the value of the coin, known as its denomination. Most coins also show the year in which they were made. Around the edge of both faces is a slightly raised ring called the rim, which protects the design from wear and allows coins to be stacked neatly. The edge itself may be smooth, or it may have a pattern of small lines known as milling.

Milling has an interesting history. In the past, coins were made of valuable metals such as silver and gold, and dishonest people used to cut small amounts of metal from the edges. The metal could then be sold, while the coin was still spent at its full value. Milled edges made this practice easy to detect, because a damaged edge would be obvious at once. In England, the scientist Isaac Newton, who worked at the Royal Mint for around thirty years, became famous for his efforts to catch people who damaged or copied coins. Today coins are made from cheaper metals, but milling is still used, partly to help blind people tell coins apart by touch.

The production process begins with long strips of metal, which are rolled until they are exactly the right thickness. Round discs called 'blanks' are then punched out of the strips, rather like a cook cutting biscuits from dough. The blanks are heated in a furnace to make the metal softer, and then washed and dried so that they shine. Next, they pass through a machine that raises the rim. Finally, each blank is placed in a press, where two dies — hard metal tools carrying the designs — strike it from both sides at the same time with enormous force. A modern press can produce several hundred coins a minute.

Finished coins are inspected, often by cameras, to find any faulty ones, which are melted down and used again. The good coins are counted by machine and packed in bags before being sent to banks. Some coins, however, are never meant to be spent. Mints also produce special coins for collectors, which are struck more slowly and handled with gloves so that they remain in perfect condition. Worn and damaged coins that return from banks are also removed from use, melted down and turned into new metal.

intro: Section 2 — bitta gapiruvchining kundalik mavzudagi nutqi (monolog): ekskursiya, yangi xizmatlar haqida ma'lumot, yig'ilishdagi e'lon. 6.0 darajasida u odatda ikki savol turidan iborat; bu unitda — matching (ro'yxatdan harf tanlash) va chizma (diagram labelling).

Tayyorlanish vaqtini ikkiga bo'ling. Matching uchun: har savolning kalit g'oyasini tagiga chizing ("a branch on the CAMPUS", "a FREE GIFT for NEW customers", "special interest rates for STUDENTS") va ro'yxatdagi nomlarni bir marta ovoz chiqarmay o'qing. Chizma uchun: sarlavha (DEBIT CARD), old va orqa tomon, berilgan yorliqlar va bo'shliq qaysi joyda ekanini ko'ring.

Matching tuzog'i: gapiruvchi ro'yxatdagi deyarli HAMMA nomni tilga oladi. Evergreen ham sovg'a beradi, lekin faqat £5,000 dan ortiq balans uchun — bu "yangi mijozlarga" sovg'a emas. Savoldagi shartni (new customers, students, certain customers) har doim tekshiring.

Reja o'zgarishi iboralari: "we thought about putting it on the front wall ... but decided against that", "used to be", "instead", "actually". Ulardan keyin keladigan ma'lumot — javob; oldingisi — tuzoq.
Matching'da ro'yxatda ortiqcha variantlar bor (6 ta harf, 4 ta savol) — ba'zi harflar umuman ishlatilmaydi. Har savolga faqat BITTA harf yoziladi.

Chizma: gapiruvchi odatda mantiqiy tartibda yuradi (old tomon → orqa tomon → yana old) va savol raqamlari audio tartibida keladi. Joylashuv so'zlarini kuting: "at the top", "halfway down on the right", "on the back", "in the bottom right-hand corner", "just above", "to the left of".
Berilgan yorliqlar — yo'l ko'rsatkich. "Cardholder's name" eshitilsa, yaqinida 8 yoki 9 javobi bor. Bitta bo'shliqni o'tkazib yuborsangiz — to'xtamang, keyingi yorliqni kuting.
formulas: CAMPUS, FREE GIFT for NEW, STUDENTS
presentation: Gapiruvchi uchta bankni aytdi. Qaysi birini yozaman?
Savoldagi shartga to'liq mos kelganini. "Near the university" — ikki bank; "inside the university buildings" — faqat bittasi.
Ro'yxatdagi harf ikki marta ishlatiladimi?
Bu savolda — yo'q, "Choose FOUR answers". Ba'zi Section 3 matching savollarida harf takrorlanishi mumkin — ko'rsatmani o'qing.
"Lifts" eshitdim, ro'yxatda "elevators" bor.
Bu paraphrase: lift (BrE) = elevator (AmE). Ro'yxat deyarli har doim boshqa so'z bilan yoziladi.
Chizmada qaysi bo'shliqdan boshlayman?
Eng kichik raqamdan. Audio savol raqamlari tartibida keladi, chizmadagi joylashuv tartibida emas.
"Black" chizmada bor. Javobga yozamanmi?
Yo'q. Yorliqda bor so'zni takrorlamang: "black ___" → "magnetic strip".
Matching va chizma orasida pauza bo'ladimi?
Section 2 da ko'pincha qisqa pauza bor. Shu paytda chizmaga qayting va birinchi bo'shliqni toping.

why: "Only one – Finley's – actually has an office inside one of the university buildings". Tuzoq: Great Western va Moneysafe — "branches near the university".

"With International Union, you'll get a phone when you open your first account". Tuzoq: Evergreen laptopi — faqat £5,000 dan ortiq balans 9 oy saqlansa; Moneysafe va Northern Star — "if you put money on deposit".

"Moneysafe actually say that if you're in credit, your account won't cost a thing". "Certain customers" = hisobida puli borlar. Tuzoq: Evergreen, Finley's, Northern Star — "charge the same across the board".

listenings.title: Jony Academy mashqi: Greenfield Supermarket — new services
intro: Supermarket menejeri xaridorlarga yangi xizmatlar joylashuvini va o'z-o'ziga xizmat ko'rsatish kassasini tushuntiradi. Ustoz skriptni oddiy tezlikda BIR MARTA o'qiydi.
Tayyorlanish: 30 soniya Q1–4 (kalit g'oya), 30 soniya chizma (Q5–10). Ko'rsatma: ONE OR TWO WORDS for each answer.
transcript: MANAGER: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming to this short talk. As you know, Greenfield Supermarket has just been redesigned, so I'd like to explain where you can find some of our new services, and then show you how our self-service checkouts work.

MANAGER: Let's start with returns. If something you've bought is faulty, you might expect to take it back to the checkout where you paid. Please don't — the checkout staff are very busy. Instead, go to the customer service desk, which is just on your right as you come in. They'll give you a refund or a replacement.

MANAGER: Now, online orders. Until last month, you collected these from a counter by the main entrance, but that area was getting far too crowded. So now there's a collection point in the car park, next to the trolley shelter. You can drive right up to it, and a member of staff will put the bags in your car.

MANAGER: A lot of you have asked about photo printing. We did think about putting the photo machines in the café, so people could have a coffee while they wait, but there simply wasn't enough space. So you'll find them on the first floor, next to the pharmacy.

MANAGER: And finally, recycling. The bottle machines used to be in the car park, but people told us they didn't like carrying bags of bottles across it in the rain. So we've moved them to just inside the main entrance. You put your empty plastic bottles in, and you get a voucher to spend in the store.

MANAGER: Right, now let's look at the self-service checkouts. If you look at the picture on the screen here... The first thing you'll see is the large touch screen. Before you start scanning, you need to choose your language — we have English, Uzbek and Russian — because all the instructions after that will appear in the language you pick. Some people press 'Start' straight away, but please choose the language first.

MANAGER: Below the screen is the scanner. It's a flat glass surface with a red line across it, and it reads the barcodes on your items. You don't need to press anything — just hold the barcode over the glass until you hear a beep.

MANAGER: When an item has been scanned, you put it in the bagging area on the right. Underneath the bags there are scales, which check the weight of everything you put down. If the weight doesn't match the item you've scanned, the machine will stop and ask you to wait for help. So please don't put your handbag or your coat in the bagging area!

MANAGER: When you've finished, you pay. On the right, below the scanner, there's the card reader. As well as bank cards, it also accepts phones, so if you have a payment app, you can simply hold your phone over it. It doesn't take watches yet, although we're hoping to add that next year.
MANAGER: If you prefer cash, coins go in the small tray at the bottom, and notes go in the long slot on the left, just under the scanner. Your change will come out of the same tray as your coins.

MANAGER: Last of all, you'll notice a light on top of each machine. While you're scanning, it stays green. If there's a problem, or if you're buying something that needs an age check, it turns yellow, and one of our assistants will come over straight away. Don't worry if it flashes red for a second when the machine starts up — that's just the system checking itself.
MANAGER: Right, if you'd like to try one now, please follow me to the checkout area.

intro: IELTS 6.0 darajasida Passage 2 da ko'pincha uch xil savol turi keladi. Bugungi kombinatsiya: Matching headings (1–6), Matching features (7–10) va Sentence completion (11–13). Uchalasining TARTIB qoidasi har xil — shuni bilish vaqtni tejaydi.

Matching headings — xatboshilar A, B, C... tartibida keladi, sarlavhalar ro'yxati esa aralash. Har xatboshiga bitta sarlavha, ro'yxatda 2–3 ta ortiqcha sarlavha bor. Sarlavha xatboshining ASOSIY g'oyasini beradi, bitta gapini emas.

Matching features — gaplar (7–10) matn tartibida EMAS. Variantlar ro'yxati (odamlar, tajribalar, guruhlar) matnda turli joyda uchraydi. Shuning uchun birinchi ish — variantlarni matnda topib, tagiga chizish. "You may use any letter more than once" — ba'zi harf ikki marta, ba'zisi umuman ishlatilmasligi mumkin.

Sentence completion — gaplar matn tartibida keladi (ALWAYS). Gapdagi kalit so'z bilan joyni toping, javobni matndan AYNAN ko'chiring. So'z chegarasi: ONE WORD ONLY — faqat bitta so'z; "their feelings" yoki "real clues" — 0 ball.

Qaysi tartibda ishlash kerak? Tavsiya: 1) 1 daqiqa xarita — uch guruhni ko'zdan kechiring, sarlavhalardagi kalit so'zlarni va features variantlarini (Koko, children, TV programme) belgilang. 2) Matnni xatboshima-xatbosh o'qing: har xatboshidan keyin sarlavha tanlang va shu xatboshida qaysi variant (A/B/C) borligini chetiga yozing. 3) Features gaplarini belgilangan joylar bilan solishtiring. 4) Sentence completion — oxirida, tartib bilan skanerlab.

Headings tuzog'i: xatboshidagi bitta tafsilot sarlavhaga mos kelib qoladi ("detail trap") yoki sarlavhadagi so'z matnda aynan uchraydi. Masalan, SB D xatboshida "liars ... do not appear nervous" bor — bu yolg'onchilar nima QILISHI emas, odamlarning noto'g'ri ishonchi haqida.
Vaqt: Passage 2 ga 20 daqiqa. Taxminan: xarita — 1, headings — 8, features — 5, sentence completion — 4, tekshirish va transfer — 2 daqiqa.
formulas: Har xatbosh chetiga variant harfini yozing
Sentence completion — tartib bilan, aynan ko'chirish
presentation: Headings'ni birinchi qilamanmi yoki oxirida?
Xatboshini o'qiyotganda darhol qiling — keyin qayta o'qish shart bo'lmaydi. Qiyin xatboshini belgilab o'tib keting.
Features'da bitta harf ikki marta chiqdi. Xatomi?
Yo'q. "You may use any letter more than once" — bu normal. Ba'zi harf umuman ishlatilmasligi ham mumkin.
Features gaplari matn tartibidami?
Yo'q. Shuning uchun variantlarni oldindan tagiga chizish kerak — gapni variant joylari bilan solishtirasiz.
Sarlavhadagi so'z xatboshida bor. Demak shu sarlavhami?
Shart emas. Butun xatbosh shu haqidami — tekshiring. Bir xil so'z ko'pincha tuzoq.
"nervous" o'rniga "nervously" yozsam bo'ladimi?
Yo'q. Bo'shliqdan keyin "behaviour" (ot) — oldidan sifat kerak. So'z turi xato bo'lsa — 0 ball.
Sentence completion javobi matnda boshqa shaklda bo'lsa-chi?
Matndagi so'zni o'zgartirmay yozing. Agar gapga grammatik mos kelmasa — boshqa so'zni qidiring.
notes: 5.0 da matching headings (10-dars), sentence completion (15-dars) va matching features'ni alohida o'rgangan edik. Endi uchalasi bitta passage'da — asosiy ko'nikma tartib va vaqtni boshqarish.
SB matnida har xatboshidan keyin o'quvchilardan so'rang: "Asosiy g'oya nima?" va "Bu xatboshida qaysi tajriba bor?" — ikkala savolga bir vaqtda javob berishga o'rgating.
Kuchli o'quvchilarga: ishlatilmagan sarlavhalar (iii, vii) nega mos kelmasligini isbotlash.
mistakes: Xatboshidagi bitta gapga qarab sarlavha tanlash
Features'da har harfni faqat bir marta ishlatish
Harf takrorlanishi mumkin (A, C, A, B)
Bolalar yashirin kamerani bilmagan — teskari ma'no
ONE WORD ONLY — ikki so'z 0 ball

how: CORE — munosabatlar va yolg'on mavzusidagi asosiy so'zlar; STRONG — xarakter va oila; SUPER — matndagi iboralar.
Har so'z bilan o'quvchi o'z oilasi yoki do'sti haqida bitta gap tuzsin: "My younger brother is a bit spoilt."

It takes years to build trust.

Mening uchta aka-ukam va opa-singlim bor.

Oxiri bola kosani sindirganini tan oldi.

Asabiy xatti-harakat har doim ham yolg'on belgisi emas.

Aka-ukalar orasidagi raqobat juda keng tarqalgan.

Kattaroq egizak ko'pincha ustun rol oladi.
Everyone says the youngest child is spoilt.
Liars often avoid talking about themselves.
Yolg'onchilar ko'pincha o'zi haqida gapirishdan qochadi.
She avoids confrontation with her brothers.

Ovozi uning yolg'on gapirayotganini fosh qildi.
Looking away is not a tell-tale sign of lying.

class_ex.title: Nega bu javoblar xato? (SB, 4-mashq)
class_ex.instr: Bu javoblar 11–13-savollarga yozilgan va 0 ball olgan. Har biri uchun sababni ayting: so'z soni, so'z turi, imlo yoki noto'g'ri ma'lumot.
items: 11 — body language
11 — nervously
12 — their feelings
12 — themsleves
12 — feeling
13 — real clues
13 — use
why: ONE WORD ONLY — ikki so'z. Bo'shliqdan keyin "behaviour" keladi, oldidan sifat kerak, ot emas. Mazmuni ham teskari: matn aynan body language yolg'onni fosh qilmaydi deydi.
"display ___ behaviour" — otdan oldin sifat: nervous. Ravish (nervously) grammatikaga mos emas.
"their own" gapda allaqachon bor. Ikki so'z yozildi — chegara buzildi.
To'g'ri imlo "themselves". Bundan tashqari, gapda "their own" dan keyin "themselves" grammatikaga to'g'ri kelmaydi.
Matnda "several references to his feelings" — ko'plik. "feeling" — boshqa shakl.
Ikki so'z; bundan tashqari "real clues" — gapda "people's ___ rather than their movements" ga mos emas. Javob — words.
"people's ___" — egalik shaklidan keyin ot kerak. "use" bu yerda fe'l — matnda "the words that people use".
class_ex.note: Mashqdan keyin doskaga yozing: ONE WORD ONLY → 1) so'z soni, 2) so'z turi, 3) imlo, 4) gapga qo'yib qayta o'qish.

class_ex.title: Asosiy g'oya yoki tafsilot?
class_ex.instr: Ustoz qisqa xatboshini o'qiydi. O'quvchilar ikki sarlavhadan birini tanlaydi va ikkinchisi nega tuzoq ekanini aytadi.
items: "Many people believe that liars avoid eye contact. However, films of real liars show that they look at you just as often as honest people do. Our ideas about lying are often simply wrong." — A) Liars avoid eye contact  B) A common belief that is not true

"Twins often share a room, clothes and friends. As a result, it can be hard for them to develop separate identities, and parents may need to treat them as individuals." — A) Twins who share clothes  B) The challenge of being an individual

"Children begin to tell simple lies at about three. By five or six, their lies become more believable, because they understand what other people know and do not know." — A) How lying develops with age  B) Three-year-olds are honest

"The survey was repeated in 60 countries. In every place, people gave almost the same answers about how to spot a liar." — A) Surprising differences between cultures  B) Similar views around the world
why: Asosiy g'oya — oxirgi gap: fikrimiz noto'g'ri. A — xatboshidagi birinchi gap, lekin keyin rad etiladi. Bu SB D xatboshisiga o'xshaydi.
Kiyim — bitta tafsilot. Butun xatbosh egizaklarning alohida shaxs bo'lish qiyinligi haqida.
Xatbosh yosh bilan o'zgarish haqida (3 → 5–6). B — teskari: uch yoshda ham yolg'on gapiradi.
"Almost the same answers" — o'xshashlik. A — teskari ma'no tuzog'i.
class_ex.note: Har javobdan keyin so'rang: "Xatboshini bir gapda qanday aytasiz?" — o'quvchi o'z so'zi bilan aytib bera olsa, sarlavhani to'g'ri tanlaydi.

why: Gorillalar tajribasi: trenerlar "reliable evidence of intentional deceit" topgan — maymunlar ham aldaydi. vii tuzog'i: xatboshida yolg'onchi bilan "muomala" qilish haqida gap yo'q.
Bolalar tajribasi: "lying starts to emerge the moment we learn to speak" — qachon boshlanadi degan savolga javob.
TV dasturi, 30 000 dan ortiq qo'ng'iroq: "viewers were unable to tell the difference". Ommaviy sinov — public test.

"People fail to detect lies because they are basing their opinions on behaviours that are not actually associated with deception". Tuzoq i: "liars do not necessarily look away" — bu yolg'onchilar nima QILMASLIGI, asosiy g'oya noto'g'ri ishonchlar.
"Liars tend to say less and provide fewer details" va "fewer references to themselves" — yolg'onchilar aslida nima qiladi.
TV, gazeta va radio solishtiriladi: "the radio listeners scored an impressive 73% accuracy rate". Qaysi aloqa shakli yolg'onni yaxshiroq fosh qiladi.

readings.title: Practice 1: The science of friendship
readings.qtype: Matching headings (1–6) + Matching features (7–10) + Sentence completion (11–13)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 2 darajasi)
text: A Most of our close relationships are given to us. We do not choose our parents, our brothers and sisters or, in many cases, our neighbours and colleagues. Friendship is different. It is entered into freely, it is not held together by any written contract, and it can end quietly without anyone announcing it. Both people must keep choosing to continue it. Perhaps for this reason, psychologists paid it relatively little attention for much of the twentieth century, preferring to study families and romantic partners. Over the last thirty years, however, friendship has become a serious subject of research.

B One of the strongest findings concerns health. In 2010, a team of researchers combined the results of 148 earlier studies, which together had followed more than 300,000 people for several years. They found that people with strong social relationships were around 50 per cent more likely to survive over the period studied than those with weak ones. The researchers pointed out that the size of this effect was comparable to that of giving up smoking, and larger than the effect of lack of exercise. Loneliness, they argued, should therefore be treated as a public health issue rather than a purely private matter, and in recent years some governments have begun to discuss it in exactly those terms.

C How many friends can one person have? The British anthropologist Robin Dunbar approached this question by comparing monkeys and apes. He noticed that species with a larger outer layer of the brain, the part used for complex thinking, lived in larger social groups. Applying the same relationship to humans, he predicted that we can maintain about 150 meaningful relationships. Within this number, he argued, there are layers: roughly five very close friends, fifteen good friends and fifty friends we see less often. The figure of around 150 has since become known as 'Dunbar's number', although other researchers argue that it varies a great deal from one person to another.

D Other researchers have asked how friendships are formed. The American communication researcher Jeffrey Hall surveyed adults who had recently moved to a new city, as well as first-year university students. He estimated that it takes around 50 hours of shared time to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend, and more than 200 hours to become close friends. What people did together also mattered: hours spent chatting, joking and catching up increased closeness far more than hours spent working side by side. His conclusion was simple: friendship cannot be rushed, and people who move to a new place should expect the process to take months rather than weeks.

E Friendships also end, and usually not because of an argument. More often, one person moves away, changes job, marries or has children, and the two simply see each other less. Dunbar and his colleagues followed a group of students after they left school and found that when contact decreased, feelings of closeness to friends fell quite quickly. Relationships with family members, by contrast, were far more resistant to lack of contact. Friendships that survive distance tend to be those in which both people make a regular effort to call or visit.

F Can technology change these patterns? Social media allows people to keep hundreds of online friends, and it certainly helps people stay in touch across long distances. Some researchers suggest that video calls are more effective than written messages, because they allow people to see each other's faces and share a laugh. Yet research on social media users suggests that the number of people they could rely on in a crisis is still only a handful, similar to the innermost layer of Dunbar's model. It seems that the closest relationships still depend on time and, above all, on meeting face to face.
glossary: anthropologist — antropolog (inson va jamiyatni o'rganuvchi olim)
paraphrases: a larger outer layer of the brain
what people did together also mattered
relationships with family members ... far more resistant to lack of contact

readings.title: Practice 2: Good neighbours
readings.qtype: Matching headings (1–6) + Matching features (7–10) + Sentence completion (11–13)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 2 darajasi)
text: A In many large cities, it is now common for people to live next door to someone for years without learning their name. Surveys in several countries have found that a large proportion of city residents cannot name a single neighbour. Neighbourhood apps have become popular, but they are mostly used to report lost pets or complain about noise, and rarely lead to real conversations. The change is often explained by longer working hours, frequent moves and the fact that many people now work and socialise far from where they live. For many, the person on the other side of the wall has become a stranger.

B This matters for practical reasons. A neighbour can take in a parcel, keep a spare key or notice that something is wrong. During a heatwave, health services often advise people to check on older residents nearby, especially those who live alone, because they may not ask for help themselves. In an emergency, the people next door are usually closer than any friend or relative. Some research has even suggested that areas where neighbours know each other recover more quickly after floods or storms.

C Several community schemes have tried to change this. The simplest is the street party. Once a year, usually on a Sunday in summer, residents close their road to traffic and bring tables, chairs and food outside. Children are usually the first to mix, and parents often meet each other through them. Organisers must first obtain permission from the local council to close the road. In one northern town, a street party that began with thirty households has become an annual tradition, and residents say that people who met there now greet each other throughout the year.

D A second idea is the tool-sharing scheme, sometimes called a 'library of things'. Instead of each household buying a drill or a ladder that is used only a few times, members borrow items from a shared store, usually run by volunteers from a community hall. Items range from pasta machines to camping tents, and each one is checked for safety before it is lent out. Members pay a small annual fee to cover repairs. Apart from saving money and reducing waste, the organisers report an unexpected benefit: people often start conversations when they bring items back, and some end up helping each other with repairs.

E A third scheme focuses on older people who live alone. Volunteers agree to visit the same person once a week for an hour, simply to talk. Before they begin, every volunteer receives training, and visits are arranged by a coordinator. The scheme does not offer shopping or personal care; its only aim is companionship. Many of the people who receive visits have no close family nearby, and volunteers often say they gain as much from the conversations as the people they visit. Several pairs have continued to meet long after the formal arrangement ended.

F Not everyone welcomes these efforts. Some residents value their privacy and feel uncomfortable being invited to join in. Schemes also depend heavily on a few enthusiastic volunteers and often stop when those people move away. Researchers who study communities suggest that large events may matter less than small, repeated contact. In their view, a brief greeting on the stairs, repeated day after day, does more to build trust than a single party.
paraphrases: the person on the other side of the wall has become a stranger
take in a parcel, keep a spare key

readings.title: Practice 3 (uyga): Do animals have friends?
readings.qtype: Matching headings (1–6) + Matching features (7–10) + Sentence completion (11–13)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 2 darajasi), uy vazifasi
text: A For much of the twentieth century, most biologists avoided using the word 'friend' when describing animals. It seemed unscientific to suggest that animals felt affection, so researchers spoke instead of 'preferred partners' or 'social bonds'. In recent decades, however, long-term studies of animals in the wild have shown that many species form close, selective and lasting relationships, and a growing number of scientists are now willing to call them friendships. Part of the change came from simply watching the same individuals for many years, which allowed researchers to see who spent time with whom. Such bonds have now been described in species as different as elephants, horses and chimpanzees.

B Some of the clearest evidence comes from baboons. Researchers who have observed wild baboons in Africa for many years found that females spend much of their time grooming a small number of preferred companions. Grooming, in which one animal cleans another's fur, appears to be the main way these bonds are built and kept. The females with the strongest and most stable bonds had more infants that survived their first year, and later studies found that these females also tended to live longer. For a baboon, it seems, good friends are a matter of life and death.

C Vampire bats provide a very different example. These bats feed only on blood, and an adult that fails to find a meal for two or three nights may starve. A well-fed bat will often bring up some of its meal to feed a hungry member of its group, including bats that are not relatives. Experiments with captive bats showed that they were more likely to share food with individuals that had shared with them in the past. Bats that had built up a wider network of partners coped better when one partner was removed. In this way, sharing works rather like insurance: a bat that gives food today may need to receive it tomorrow.

D Among bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Western Australia, males form alliances of two or three individuals that cooperate to stay close to females. These small alliances sometimes join together into larger teams, and some partnerships last for decades. Dolphins also use individual 'signature whistles', which work rather like names, and experiments have shown that they can recognise the whistle of a former companion even after twenty years apart. Females form social networks too, although these are generally looser than the male alliances.

E Why should animals form friendships at all? Scientists point to several advantages. Friends can offer protection against predators and against aggressive members of the same group. They share food and information about where to find it. Friendships may also give access to safer resting places or a better position within the group. There is also evidence that close companions help to reduce stress: animals that lose a close partner often show a rise in stress hormones and try to form new bonds.

F Some researchers remain cautious. They warn against describing animals as if they were humans, and point out that scientists can measure behaviour, such as time spent together, but cannot observe feelings directly. Others reply that the same hormones involved in human bonding are active in other mammals. The debate is unlikely to end soon, but few now doubt that, for many animals, relationships are central to survival.
paraphrases: researchers spoke instead of 'preferred partners' ... now willing to call them friendships
more infants that survived their first year
recognise the whistle of a former companion

items: 7 Individuals can identify old companions after a long separation.
8 Some individuals help others that are not part of their family.
9 Stronger relationships were linked to more young surviving.

why: "They can recognise the whistle of a former companion even after twenty years apart".
"Including bats that are not relatives".

"Males form alliances of two or three individuals that cooperate".

tasks.title: Questions 11–13
tasks.type: Complete the sentences. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

12 A vampire bat may die if it cannot feed for two or three ___.
13 Researchers can record how animals behave but cannot directly see their ___.
why: "Researchers spoke instead of 'preferred partners'".
"An adult that fails to find a meal for two or three nights may starve".
"Scientists can measure behaviour ... but cannot observe feelings directly".

homework_intro: Bugun bitta passage'da uch savol turini birga yechdik: xarita → headings va features belgilari → sentence completion. Uyda xuddi shu tartibda yolg'iz ishlaysiz.

Birinchi vazifa — Practice 3 "Do animals have friends?": 20 daqiqa vaqt oling, 13 savolga javob bering. Har sarlavha yoniga xatboshining asosiy g'oyasini o'zbekcha bir gapda yozing, features variantlarini matnda tagiga chizing.

Ikkinchi vazifa — 30-Day Reading Challenge'dan Day 17 (Questions 14–20 matching headings va Questions 23–26 sentence completion) va Day 29 (Questions 14–20 matching headings va Questions 23–26 matching features). intro: Section 3 — o'quv mavzusidagi suhbat: odatda ikki talaba (ba'zan ustoz bilan) loyiha, taqdimot yoki tadqiqot haqida gaplashadi. Til Section 1–2 ga qaraganda murakkabroq: fikrlar almashadi, gapiruvchilar bir-birini to'g'rilaydi va rozi bo'lmaydi.

6.0 darajasida Section 3 ko'pincha ikki turdan iborat: Multiple choice (A, B, C) va flow chart (yoki notes) completion. Ular orasida odatda qisqa pauza bo'ladi — o'sha paytda ikkinchi topshiriqni yana bir bor ko'zdan kechiring.

Tayyorlanish vaqtini ikkiga bo'ling. MCQ uchun: savol o'zagidagi kalit g'oyaning tagiga chizing ("what PROBLEM", "MUST include", "arrange to") — variantlarga emas (SB 2-mashq). Flow chart uchun: har bo'shliqqa qanday so'z kerakligini yozing (ot? ko'plik? joy?) va o'qlar tartibini ko'ring — bosqichlar audioda xuddi shu tartibda keladi.

SIGNAL iboralar javob yaqinlashayotganini bildiradi: "That's the trouble...", "The thing about Mr Dresden is...", "He said that the important thing was...", "The very first thing you need to do is...", "After that...", "The next thing might be...", "Or better still...". Signalni eshitsangiz — keyingi gapga to'liq diqqat.

MCQ TUZOG'I: Section 3 da uchala variant deyarli har doim tilga olinadi. Biri rad etiladi ("Mr Dresden didn't ask for data"), biri boshqa odam yoki boshqa vaqt haqida ("I'm going to the library" — Victor, Fumiko emas). Kim gapiryapti va kim haqida — shuni tekshiring.

FLOW CHART TUZOG'I: gapiruvchi avval bir so'zni aytadi, keyin boshqasi uni to'g'rilaydi yoki yaxshiroq variant taklif qiladi: "places" → "You mean the 'contexts'? — Yes, that's the word"; "future changes" → "or better still, the influences". Oxirgi, kelishilgan so'z — javob.
Transfer: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS — "the animal world" emas, "animal world"; ko'plik -s (key terms, contexts, stages, influences) ko'p ball olib qo'yadi.
formulas: what PROBLEM / MUST include / arrange to
presentation: MCQ da uchala variant ham eshitildi. Qaysi biri?
Savol o'zagiga qayting: KIM haqida va NIMA so'ralyapti? Qolgan ikkitasi odatda rad etilgan yoki boshqa odam haqida.
Flow chart bo'shliqlari ham tartibdami?
Ha. O'qlar bosqichlar ketma-ketligini ko'rsatadi, audio ham shu tartibda boradi.
Gapiruvchi so'zni o'zgartirdi. Qaysi birini yozaman?
Oxirgi, ikkala gapiruvchi rozi bo'lgan so'zni: "Yes, that's the word", "OK, influences".
Signal ibora nima uchun kerak?
U javob yaqinlashayotganini bildiradi. Signalni eshitsangiz, savolni ko'z bilan kuzating va keyingi gapni diqqat bilan tinglang.
"the animal world" deb yozsam bo'ladimi?
Yo'q. Bo'shliq oldidan "the" allaqachon bor — faqat "animal world". Artikl ham so'z hisoblanadi.
Bitta javobni o'tkazib yubordim. Nima qilaman?
To'xtamang — keyingi bosqichga o'ting. Oxirida mantiqan eng mos so'zni yozing, bo'sh qoldirmang.
notes: 5.0 da MCQ va flow chart'ni alohida o'rgangan edik. Endi ular bitta Section 3 da ketma-ket — o'rtadagi pauzadan to'g'ri foydalanish asosiy ko'nikma.
Tekshiruvda har javobdan keyin skriptdan aynan o'sha gapni ekranga chiqaring va signal iborani boshqa rang bilan ko'rsating (SB 3- va 6-mashqlar).
Kuchli o'quvchilarga: Workbook audiosidan keyin Maya'ning jadval va diagrammalarini (1 table, 2 tables, pie chart) xotiradan sanab berish.
mistakes: C — doesn't know what to focus on
"I think I've got plenty" — ma'lumot yetarli
"Mr Dresden didn't ask for data" — rad etilgan
Victor to'g'rilaydi, Fumiko "that's the word" deydi

how: CORE — o'quv loyihasi va tadqiqot so'zlari; STRONG — ma'lumotni taqdim etish; SUPER — Section 3 dagi signal iboralar.
Har o'quvchi o'z loyihasi (maktab yoki kurs) haqida 3 gap aytadi va kamida ikkita yangi so'z ishlatadi.
core: I've got a psychology project this term.
Bu semestr menda psixologiya loyihasi bor.
My tutor gives very broad project titles.
Kuratorim loyihalarga juda keng mavzular beradi.
The project is part of my assessment.
I could do a survey of people of different ages.
Turli yoshdagi odamlar orasida so'rovnoma o'tkazishim mumkin.
Include a list of all your sources.
Start with a definition of your key terms.
Give some background on the topic first.
Avval mavzu haqida umumiy ma'lumot bering.
There are six stages in a friendship.
The subjects couldn't fill in the questionnaire.
She is nervous about her presentation.
strong: A bibliography must be included at the end.
I can't narrow the topic down.
It was only a small sample.
My sample proved to be representative.
My parents have several lifelong friends.
Ota-onamning bir necha umrbod do'sti bor.
I've presented that data in a pie chart.
super: That's the trouble — I don't know where to start.
Text me, or better still, call me.
Menga yozing, yoki undan ham yaxshisi, qo'ng'iroq qiling.
You have to limit the scope of the study.
Tell you what, I'll text you in half an hour.
Mana nima qilamiz, yarim soatdan keyin yozaman.

class_ex.title: Signal iboralar: qaysi savolga? (SB, 3-mashq)
class_ex.instr: Tinglashdan oldin: har signal ibora 1–5-savollardan qaysi biriga javob olib kelishini taxmin qiling. Tinglagandan keyin tekshiring.
items: a The thing about Mr Dresden is ...
b That's the trouble ...
c He said that the important thing was ...
d Look, tell you what, I'll text you ...
e So what reading have you done so far?
why: 2-savol — tutor haqida: "The thing about Mr Dresden is that he likes to find out what you really enjoy working on".
1-savol — muammo: "that's the trouble — I don't really know where to start".
4-savol — loyihada nima bo'lishi SHART: "the important thing was to read about the topic and definitely include a list of all our sources".
5-savol — nima kelishishdi: "I'll text you in half an hour".
3-savol — nima o'qigan: Victor savoli javob yaqinligini bildiradi.
class_ex.note: Kitobda b → 1 namuna sifatida berilgan. Mashqdan keyin doskaga signal iboralar ro'yxatini yozing — dars davomida to'ldirib boriladi.

class_ex.title: Flow chart bo'shliqlarini oldindan aytish (SB, 4-mashq)
class_ex.instr: 6–10-savollarga javob bermasdan, har bo'shliqqa qanday so'z va qanday ma'lumot kerakligini ayting.
items: 6 — "Define ___ using a diagram"
7 — "Background: relationships in the ___, e.g. apes"
8 — "Present an overview of the ___ for human relationships, e.g. work, home"
9 — "Look at six ___ involved in a friendship"
10 — "Predict the future ___ on friendship"
why: "Define" fe'lidan keyin ot — nimani ta'riflaysiz? Loyiha boshida odatda atamalar ta'riflanadi.
"the ___, e.g. apes" — maymunlar misol bo'ladigan soha yoki olam.
"e.g. work, home" — ish va uy — joy yoki vaziyat; ko'plik.
"six ___" — son, demak ko'plik -s.
"future ___ on friendship" — "on" predlogi bilan: effect on / influence on.
class_ex.note: 10-savol uchun o'quvchilar "changes" deyishi mumkin — tinglashda gapiruvchi aynan shu so'zni aytib, keyin to'g'rilaydi. Buni oldindan aytmang, tekshiruvda ko'rsating.

listenings.title: Student's Book, Track 7: Fumiko's psychology project (Q1–10)
intro: Fumiko psixologiya loyihasi haqida Victor bilan gaplashadi; ikkinchi qismda ular birga reja tuzadi. Tinglashdan oldin: 1–5 da savol o'zagidagi kalit g'oyani belgilang (SB 2-mashq), 6–10 da bo'shliq turini yozing.
Q1–5 va Q6–10 orasida qisqa pauza bor. Flow chart ko'rsatmasi: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer. Savollar sahifasi quyida rasm sifatida.

tasks.title: Questions 1–5
tasks.type: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C
tasks.instr: Uchala variant ham eshitiladi. Kim haqida va nima so'ralyapti — shuni tekshiring.
items: 1 What problem does Fumiko have with her psychology project? A) She isn't interested in the topic. B) She can't find enough information. C) She doesn't know what to focus on.
2 What point does Victor make about Fumiko's tutor? A) He explores his students' key interests. B) He is a very hard-working member of staff. C) He uses a limited range of project titles.
3 What has Fumiko already read on her topic? A) book extracts B) journal articles C) internet material
4 According to Mr Dresden, Fumiko's project must include A) some graphic data. B) a bibliography. C) a public survey.
5 Victor and Fumiko arrange to A) get in contact in half an hour. B) meet up in the library. C) have lunch together.
why: "That's the trouble — I don't really know where to start ... can't seem to narrow it down". A — tuzoq: "I'm really enjoying it"; B — "I think I've got plenty" (g'oyalar yetarli).
"The thing about Mr Dresden is that he likes to find out what you really enjoy working on". C — tuzoq: u "broad" (keng) mavzular beradi, cheklangan emas.
"Have you been on the Internet? — I have, and there are some fascinating reports". A — kitoblarni endi olgan, hali o'qimagan; B — jurnal maqolalarini "put them away ... without looking at them".
"Definitely include a list of all our sources" = bibliography. A — tuzoq: "Mr Dresden didn't ask for data"; C — so'rovnoma Fumiko'ning o'z g'oyasi.
"Tell you what, I'll text you in half an hour". B — kutubxonaga Victor yolg'iz boradi; C — kofe va faqat seminar tez tugasa, tushlik emas.
tasks.note: 5-savol yaxshi misol: "library" va "canteen" ikkalasi ham eshitiladi, lekin aniq kelishilgan narsa — yarim soatdan keyin xabar yozish.

tasks.title: Questions 6–10 — Fumiko's plan
tasks.type: Complete the flow chart. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: O'qlar tartibi = suhbat tartibi. Victor Fumiko'ning so'zini to'g'rilaganda yaxshi tinglang.
why: "The very first thing you need to do is give a definition of what you mean by your key terms". "Using a diagram" = "you could just do a diagram".
"You could do a bit of background on the animal world ... relationships among ape groups". "the" formada bor — ikki so'z yoziladi.
Fumiko "places" deydi, Victor: "You mean the 'contexts' for relationships" — "Yes, that's the word". Kalitda — contexts.
"Why don't you go through the stages in a friendship? ... just select six".
"Maybe the future changes in ... — Yeah, or better still, the influences". "changes" — tuzoq.
tasks.note: 8 va 10-savol — Section 3 ning asosiy tuzog'i: birinchi aytilgan so'z emas, tuzatilgan so'z javob.
rows: Background: relationships in the (7), e.g. apes
Present an overview of the (8) for human relationships, e.g. work, home
Look at six (9) involved in a friendship (plus survey)

tasks.title: 6-mashq: signal so'zlar (qayta tinglab)
tasks.type: Bitta so'z yozing
tasks.instr: Track 7 ning ikkinchi qismini qayta tinglang va har signal iboradagi bo'shliqni to'ldiring. Bu iboralar 6–10-javoblardan oldin keladi.
items: 6 I think the very ___ thing you need to do is ...
7 After ___, you could do ...
8 'You mean ... ?' 'Yes, ___ the word.'
9 The ___ thing might be to ...
10 Why don't I ___ by ..., or better still, ...
why: "I think the very first thing you need to do is give a definition..."
"Right. After that, you could do a bit of background..."
"You mean the 'contexts' for relationships. — Yes, that's the word."
"Or the next thing might be to select one type of relationship..."
"Why don't I end by looking into the future? — Yeah, or better still, the influences".
tasks.note: Kitobda bu mashq uchun alohida CD2 Track 8 bor; bu yerda o'sha qism Track 7 dan qayta eshittiriladi.

listenings.title: Student's Book: recording script (CD2 Track 7) — ustoz uchun
intro: Tekshiruvdan keyin ekranga chiqaring. Har javob gapini, signal iborani va tuzoq gapni alohida rang bilan ko'rsating.

listenings.title: Workbook, Track 8: Maya's presentation on lifelong friendships (Q1–10)
listenings.qtype: Multiple choice + Flow chart — imtihon rejimi
intro: Jack va Maya Maya'ning taqdimoti haqida gaplashadi: avval tadqiqot qanday o'tgani (MCQ), keyin taqdimot tuzilishi (flow chart). Avval Workbook 1-mashqini bajaring.
Keyin imtihondagidek: tayyorlanish vaqti, audio BIR MARTA, 10 savol. Flow chart: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS.

tasks.title: 1-mashq: 6–10 uchun qanday so'z kerak?
tasks.type: Choose A, B or C
tasks.instr: Tinglashdan oldin flow chart'ni ko'zdan kechiring.
items: 1 What kind of word will be required for all of Questions 6–10? A) adverbs B) verbs C) nouns
why: "change of ___", "Effects of ___", "descriptions of ___", "Changes in ___" — predlogdan keyin ot; 10 esa sarlavha ("___ (e.g. sports, musical tastes)") — ham ot.

tasks.title: Questions 1–5
tasks.type: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C
tasks.instr: Maya har savolda bir nechta narsani aytadi — savol o'zagidagi kalit g'oyaga mos kelganini tanlang.
items: 1 Maya chose the topic of lifelong friendships because A) it was an unusual area of research. B) she had a particular interest in it. C) someone suggested it to her.
2 Maya says that the sample of people she used A) was smaller than she wanted it to be. B) was typical of the population in general. C) was the basis for further work.
3 The problem with the questionnaire was that A) it wasn't well constructed. B) the subjects couldn't engage with it. C) too much time was required to complete it.
4 Maya says that when she conducted the interviews, A) she kept brief notes. B) the subjects were all very relaxed. C) they followed a clear structure.
5 What does Maya say about other research in the area? A) A lot of it contradicted her findings. B) It wasn't very easy to find. C) It was carried out in the same way as hers.
why: "There's been a lot of research on how people form friendships ... but there's not much on this particular topic". B — tuzoq: ota-onasining do'stlari — bu tadqiqot usuli, sabab emas.

"I'd collate the results from that small sample so that I could compare them with more general conclusions from research". A — "small" ni Jack aytadi, Maya norozi emas; B — "representative" keyinroq, taqqoslash natijasi haqida.
"They just couldn't analyse their friendships in that 'cold' way". C — tuzoq: "they hadn't had time" — bahona edi.
"I adapted my questionnaire and sat down with each person" — intervyu anketa asosida, aniq tuzilma bilan. A — tuzoq: yozib olgan, "rather than having to write notes".
"There's not a lot of that, but I managed to locate some academic research". A — tuzoq: "one or two disparities", lekin umuman "confirmed what I found".
tasks.note: 4-savol eng qiyin: "structure" so'zi eshitilmaydi. Anketani moslashtirib, har odam bilan u bo'yicha gaplashgan — shuning uchun intervyu tuzilmali bo'lgan.

tasks.title: Questions 6–10 — Lifelong friendships presentation
tasks.type: Complete the flow chart. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
tasks.instr: Har bosqichda Maya kategoriya nomini aytadi va qanday ko'rsatganini (table / pie chart) qo'shadi.
why: "The first category I've called 'Change of Location' ... goes to live somewhere else"; "a couple of separate tables" = 2 tables.
"What happens to the friendship when one or both of the friends get married" — "That's a pie chart".
"The next one concerns 'Personality' ... I picked out the most extreme changes".
"How much people had in common in terms of political opinions ... I've constructed another pie chart".
"I've categorised this as 'Shared Interests' ... sports doesn't change ... whereas their musical tastes do".
tasks.note: 7-savolda "married" (fe'l) emas, "marriage" (ot) yoziladi: "Effects of ___" — predlogdan keyin ot. 1-mashqdagi "nouns" javobi shu yerda yordam beradi.
rows: Origins of friendship (age, where began, circumstances, etc.): 1 table
Comparisons between descriptions of (8): patterns of extreme change
(10) (e.g. sports, musical tastes): continuing or changing

listenings.title: Workbook: recording script (Track 8) — ustoz uchun
intro: Skript bilan qayta tinglashda xato qilingan savollarning gapini topishga ishlatiladi. Jack'ning bosqichlarni almashtiruvchi savollarini ("OK, what comes next?", "What then?") belgilang.

listenings.title: Jony Academy mashqi: Friendship project
intro: Ben va Sara — sotsiologiya talabalari — birinchi kurs talabalarining do'st orttirishi haqidagi loyihani rejalashtiradi. Ustoz ikki rolni o'qiydi (yoki kuchli o'quvchi bilan). BIR MARTA.
1–5 va 6–10 orasida 20 soniya pauza qiling. Flow chart: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
transcript: BEN: Hi Sara. Have you got a minute to talk about our sociology project?
SARA: Sure, I was going to message you anyway. Have you decided on the focus?
BEN: Well, at first I wanted to look at friendship in general, but Dr Hughes said that was far too wide. So I thought we could look at how first-year students make friends in their first term.
SARA: That sounds manageable. But why first-years?
BEN: Partly because they're easy to find — they're all around us. But mainly because nobody in our department has studied them before. Dr Hughes checked the list of past projects for me.
SARA: Great. And what did he say about the length?

BEN: The written report can be up to three thousand words, but the thing he really stressed was the presentation. It mustn't go over fifteen minutes — he'll stop us if it does. He said he doesn't mind if we don't have many statistics.
SARA: Fifteen minutes isn't much. What about collecting the data? I assumed we'd do an online questionnaire.
BEN: I thought so too, but online surveys get very few replies. My cousin tried one last year and got eleven answers out of two hundred.
SARA: Wow. So what then — interviews?
BEN: Interviews take ages. I think the best option is a short paper questionnaire that we hand out at the start of lectures. Students fill it in on the spot.
SARA: OK. I'm a bit worried about one thing, though. Some students might not want to write about their friends. It's quite personal.
BEN: True. That's why we should make it anonymous — no names at all. And we'll keep it to ten questions, so it's quick.
SARA: And will lecturers let us use their time?
BEN: I've already asked two of them, and they're both happy to give us the first five minutes.
SARA: Perfect. Shall we meet on Thursday to write the questions?
BEN: Thursday's difficult — I've got a seminar all afternoon. How about Wednesday morning, in the café next to the library?
SARA: Wednesday's fine, but that café's always so noisy. Let's book one of the study rooms in the library instead.
BEN: Good idea. I'll book one tonight.
(Pause — 20 seconds)
SARA: Right, let's put the stages in order. What comes first?
BEN: I think the very first thing is to find out what other people have already written. Dr Hughes wants a short literature review — just two or three pages.
SARA: Fine. After that, we write the questions. Should we just use them straight away?
BEN: No — Dr Hughes said we should test them first on a small group. He called it a pilot study.
SARA: Who with? Our flatmates?
BEN: They're second-years, so no. It should be people like our real sample — maybe five first-years from the sports club.
SARA: OK. Then we hand out the questionnaires. We're aiming for two hundred, aren't we?
BEN: Yes. And the next stage is putting all the answers into a spreadsheet. That'll take a while.
SARA: I can do that — I'm quite quick at typing. Then we look for patterns. For example, do students who live in halls make friends faster than students who live at home?
BEN: Exactly — that comparison could be the most interesting part. And we finish with recommendations — what the university could do to help new students. Maybe more social events in the first week?
SARA: Or better still, a buddy scheme, where every new student gets a second-year partner. I think that would help most.
BEN: Agreed. Let's make that our main recommendation.
